blocks.h: A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
This book started with a fact I could not put down.

There is no file. When you remember someone, you are not opening a drawer and looking at a photograph. You are building the person, that instant, out of parts kept in different rooms — and when you are finished, what goes back into storage is not what you took out. It is what you just made. Every act of remembering is an act of writing over.

This is not damage. It is the design. It is how anyone learns that the dog which bit them is dead now. But it means something that I have not been able to stop turning over, which is that the people we have lost are not preserved in us. They are in our custody, and custody has costs, and the more often we go in to look at them, the further they travel from whatever they actually were.

The other thing I could not put down is older and simpler. A body keeps a ledger. It keeps it whether or not the mind is willing to read it, and it keeps it accurately, and it does not care that the total is unpayable. There is a long tradition of people going looking for the truth in the body when the mind has stopped cooperating — through fasting, through cold, through distance, through pain. Sometimes they come back with something. That possibility interests me enormously and I have never once been able to persuade myself that it is safe.
So: a man who has lost his wife, and one door, and a price list.

I owe a debt in these pages to Vonnegut, who taught me that the most unbearable material in a life is best carried in the plainest possible voice and with a joke close to hand. Sean Vardy is profane and he is funny and he stays funny long past the point where the rest of him has come apart. That is not decoration. In my experience it is frequently the last faculty standing, and it is worth asking what it is doing down there, holding the lights on, after everything above it has gone dark.
I have tried to be accurate about the injuries. Not for the shock of it — though there is shock in it — but because a man who is spending himself ought to be made to itemise the receipt.
Chew Z

PART ONE: THE ROOM ABOVE THE BAR
1. Ladies and Gentlemen

The banquet hall in Berwyn had a chandelier the size of a dishwasher and a carpet the color of a bad decision, and somebody had pushed the round tables against the wall to make room for the ring, which was not a ring. It was four rolls of blue gym mat duct-taped together and a rope run through eyebolts screwed into the drywall by a man who did not own a stud finder. The eyebolts were going to come out. Everybody in the room knew the eyebolts were going to come out. That was part of the ticket price.

I sat on a folding chair by the kitchen doors with my hands in my lap, unwrapped, because Denny wraps late. Denny has always wrapped late. Denny believes that a wrapped hand starts to swell inside the wrap the second you finish, that you have about eleven minutes of a hand being a hand and then it becomes a sausage in a casing, and he is not wrong, and he has also never once wrapped a hand in under nine minutes in his life, so the whole philosophy is a beautiful piece of horseshit he built to explain why he is slow. "Look at me," he said. "I'm looking at you." "You're looking at the fucking floor."
"The floor's better looking than you, Denny. The floor's got a lot going on."

He got down on one knee in front of the chair, which at sixty-something and with that hip is a whole production, an act of civil engineering, and he took my chin in his hand and turned my face toward the light. He wasn't checking my eyes. He was checking the brow. There's a scar over my left eye that runs about an inch and a quarter on the diagonal, and it has been opened nine times, and it will open again, because scar tissue is not skin. Skin stretches. Scar tissue is a repair, and a repair has no give in it, and when the fist comes it doesn't stretch, it splits, along the old line, every single time, like a shirt that's been sewn shut over a wound. "You get cut, you tell me," he said. "I get cut, you'll fucking see it, it's on my face."
"You get cut and I'm not there, you sit down. You don't get up until I'm there." "Okay."
"Say it."
"I'll sit on the floor in a banquet hall in Berwyn and wait for a sixty-four-year-old man to walk across the room. That's my whole plan for the evening, Denny. That's the strategy."

He didn't laugh. He hasn't laughed at anything I've said since the funeral, and I keep saying things anyway, which is either loyalty or a nervous condition, hard to say. He started on the left hand. Gauze, two turns at the wrist, thumb loop, the whole liturgy.

There were maybe ninety people in that room. Guys in good jackets who'd come out from the city because somebody at work told them about it and it sounded like a story they could tell. Guys in bad jackets who came every time. A few women, mostly attached to the jackets. Two kids who couldn't have been nineteen, standing right up at the rope, holding phones they had been told to put away and had not put away, and they were going to film it, and it was going to go nowhere, and in eleven years one of them would find it on an old drive and not be able to remember whose party it was.

I was forty-four years old. I had a professional record of nineteen and four and one and a detached retina that ended it, and a house in Hegewisch with a mortgage on it and a wife in the ground four years, and I was about to fight a thirty-one-year-old bricklayer named Marcus Wiley for eight hundred dollars in cash in a room that smelled like Sterno and carpet shampoo.
I want to be honest about this part, because the rest of it gets less honest as it goes, and I'd like there to be at least one thing in here you can stand on.

That night, I wasn't looking for anything. I hadn't found it yet. I didn't know it was there to be found. That night I just needed eight hundred dollars and I needed to be somewhere that wasn't the house, and those are the two most ordinary reasons a man has ever done anything, and if you're waiting for me to tell you I walked in there with a plan, I didn't.
I walked in there empty. Which, it turns out, is how you carry something out.
2. Eight Hundred Dollars

Wiley came out fast because thirty-one-year-olds come out fast. That's not a criticism. At thirty-one your body still returns your calls. Round one. He threw a jab at my chest, which is what men do when they've been taught by YouTube and one summer at a gym in Cicero — they aim at the middle of you because the middle of you is the biggest part and it feels like the safe bet. I let it land. It felt like being shoved by a door. Then he threw the right hand and I wasn't there for it, and the beautiful thing about being forty-four with nineteen wins is that I don't have to be fast anymore, I only have to be early, and early is a thing you can still do when fast is gone. I put a jab into his mouth. Not hard. A tap. Just to introduce myself, just to let him know there was a person in here with him and not a heavy bag with a face drawn on it.

He blinked. That's the moment. Everything after the first honest punch is negotiation. Round two. He got his weight into a left hook that caught me high on the temple and the room went briefly two-dimensional, like a photograph of a room, and then it came back. That's normal. That's a Tuesday. I stepped in and put a right hand under his elbow into the floating ribs, that soft ugly place where the ribs stop being a cage and start being a suggestion, and he made a noise like a man sitting down in a hot bath.

Body shots don't look like anything. That's why nobody claps. Ninety people paid to see a face come apart and the entire actual craft of this thing is happening a foot below where they're looking. You break a man's ribs and the crowd checks their phone.

He held me. His forearm came up under my chin and mashed my mouthguard sideways into my cheek and I felt the inside of my mouth open up on the molars, that clean bright little tear, and the blood came in and I swallowed it, because you swallow it, because if you spit it the referee looks at you, and the referee that night was a guy named Vito who owned two Subways. Round three. He was tired. Tired makes people brave in the worst way — they stop stepping and start swinging, because swinging feels like doing something and stepping feels like waiting. He swung. I slipped it by two inches and came over the top with the right hand and hit him flush on the button, the shelf of the jaw right at the end, the place where the whole architecture of a man is held together by one hinge on each side.

Here is what happens. The punch doesn't hurt him. That's the thing nobody understands. The punch rotates his head, and his head rotates faster than the thing inside it, and the thing inside it is not bolted down, it's floating in a bath of fluid inside a box of bone, and it keeps going after the box stops, and it hits the inside wall of the box, and then it comes back and hits the other wall. Two impacts. One punch. Every time.

He went down on his side with his eyes open. That's the worst kind and it's the kind the crowd loves best, because the eyes are open and the lights are on and there's nobody home, and for about four seconds a man is a house with the front door swinging.

They counted him out. Somebody's cousin poured water on his neck. He came back up through it slowly, the way they do, hand on the mat, face doing that confused thing, that terrible mild look of a man in a hallway trying to remember which apartment.
Vito lifted my arm. The two kids filmed it. One of the eyebolts came out of the drywall and nobody noticed.

Denny got a swab of adrenaline into the split on my brow — it had opened in the second, along the old line, obviously, hello again — and pressed it with two fingers and said nothing, and I sat on the folding chair and looked at Wiley across the room, sitting on his own folding chair, having water poured into him by a woman in a green dress. "He's fine," Denny said. "I know he's fine." "You're looking at him like he's not fine."
"I'm looking at him," I said, "because he's got a nicer chair."

I got eight hundred dollars in an envelope from a man in a Blackhawks jacket and drove home with my hands throbbing in time with the turn signal and my mouth full of the taste of a penny, and I did not think about my wife once that entire night, and I want that in the record, because it's the last time it was ever true.
3. The Week After

Here's what the week after looks like, since nobody films that part. Day one. You wake up and you can't open the left eye. Not swollen shut — that's day two. Day one it's glued. There's blood dried in the lashes and lymph fluid dried on top of the blood and the whole apparatus has set overnight like a cheap epoxy. You do not pull it. Men pull it. Men pull it and take the lashes and half the eyelid margin with them and then they've got a cut on an eyelid, which is a cut on the thinnest skin on the human body, and now they've got a real problem. What you do is you get a washcloth as hot as the tap goes, and you hold it on the whole side of your face for four minutes by the clock, and you let it dissolve, and then the eye comes open on its own and you look at yourself in a bathroom mirror at six in the morning and there is a stranger there with a purple bag under one eye like he's smuggling a plum. Day one, continued. You piss and it's brown. Not red — brown, like weak tea, like the bottom of a coffee pot. That's muscle. That's the body dissolving whatever got hit hard enough to die and flushing it out through the kidneys, and if it's dark for more than two days you're supposed to go to a hospital, and no one goes to a hospital, and the kidneys sort it out or they don't. Day two. The face has now committed. Everything that was going to swell has swelled. Under the eye is a shade of purple I have never seen anywhere else in the natural world — there's a green in it, and a kind of yellow-brown at the edge like a coffee ring — and the whole cheek has a shine, and when you press it with a finger, which you will, because you always do, the finger goes in and stays for a second before the flesh comes back. That's the tissue full of fluid. Denny calls that the pudding stage.

The hands are worse than the face and this is always true and nobody believes it. The face is one bone in one place. The hands are twenty-seven bones each, and every single one of them has just been used as a hammer by an animal that did not design them for that. The knuckles are split — not cut, split, the skin has burst outward from the pressure underneath — and the third and fourth are the size of grapes, and there's a deep ache down in the wrist where the shock went, and in the morning you cannot make a fist and you cannot hold a coffee cup and you drink out of the cup with two hands like a toddler, standing at your own kitchen counter, forty-four years old.

Day three. The bruise starts migrating. This is the part that gets everybody. Blood has weight. It obeys gravity like everything else, so it drains downward through the soft tissue overnight, and the bruise that was under your eye on Tuesday is along your jawline on Thursday and in your neck by Saturday, and you look worse on day six than you did on day two, which means every person who sees you assumes it just happened, and you have to keep saying no, this is the old one, this is fine, this is the healing, and they nod and look at your shoes. Day four. Somebody at the Jewel on Torrence asks if you're okay. She's about sixty and she's got that look, that specific expression, and I know exactly what she's seeing because I've seen it — she thinks somebody did this to me. She's got a whole story running. And I say I'm a boxer, and she says oh, thank God, and then she hears herself say it and we both stand there in the produce section holding that sentence between us like a dropped plate. Day six. The brow is knitting. You can feel it doing it. There's an itch under the scab that isn't on the skin, it's under the skin, in the meat, and it is the single most maddening sensation available to a human being. Denny used to say scratch a healing cut and you'll open it and then it'll heal wider, and a wider scar splits easier next time, and that's how a man's face turns into a road map over twenty years. One good scar. Nine bad reopenings. Day nine. You look almost normal. There's a yellow ghost under the eye. The knuckles have scabbed over black. You can make a fist again. You've slept maybe four hours a night the whole week because a bruised face has no comfortable side, and the tiredness has gotten down into the parts of you that talk, and everything you say for a week comes out flat and mean, and there's nobody in the house to say it to.
That's the week. That's what eight hundred dollars costs, arithmetic-wise.

The thing is, I'd have done it for nothing. That's not tough-guy talk. Look at the numbers. Ninety people, eight hundred bucks, four hours round trip, a face I couldn't take to a job interview for two weeks. Nobody does that for money. Anybody telling you they do it for money is telling you the first thing they thought of.
You do it because for eleven minutes on a Saturday nothing in your head is talking. That's it. That's the whole product.
4. A Man Who Knows a Face

Denny Fewster owned a two-flat in South Deering with a garage he'd turned into a gym in 1994, and by gym I mean a heavy bag, a speed bag platform he'd built out of a cabinet door, a mirror from a dead motel, and a space heater that had been recalled.
I went over on the Sunday because he'd have come to me otherwise and I didn't want him in the house.
"Jesus," he said, when he opened the door. "You look like a thumb." "Thanks." "No, but with a face drawn on it." "Thank you, Denny."

He made coffee in a machine older than my career and we sat on two folding chairs in the garage with the heater ticking and I let him look at the brow, and he took the butterflies off and looked underneath and put new ones on, and he did it with the pad of his thumb, very lightly, and it occurred to me — not for the first time — that Denny Fewster had touched my face more gently over thirty years than any man had ever touched anything of mine. "Gaz called me," he said. "Gaz calls everybody."

"He's got a card at the VFW in Cicero the second week of December. Eight hundred, gloved, three by three." He turned the mug around in his hands. "And then he did the other thing he does." "What's the other thing he does." "He talked about bare."

Gaz Tunney was not a gangster and I want to be clear about that, because it would be a great comfort to me now if he had been. Gaz was five foot six and wore a quarter-zip and had a phone in each hand and a spreadsheet with tabs, and he had never in his life made a man do anything. That's the whole problem with Gaz. He was a facilitator. You told Gaz what you wanted and Gaz went and got it, promptly, at a fair price, with a text message confirming, and if what you wanted was to be beaten to death in stages then Gaz would find you a room and forty guys to watch and he would not think about it once, not because he was cruel, but because he was in logistics. "I'm not doing bare," I said.
"Good."
"I'm forty-four years old, Denny. My hands are the last thing I've got that works."
Which was true, and which was also, I understand now, the exact sound a man makes standing at the edge of a thing and describing the edge in detail so he doesn't have to describe the thing.

Because let me tell you what bare actually is, since everybody gets it wrong. People hear bare-knuckle and they think: more savage. And it is, but not the way they think. The glove was never there to protect the man getting hit. It's there to protect the fist. Take the padding off and your hand becomes the fragile part — the fifth metacarpal, the long bone behind your little finger, goes at a fraction of the force a grown man can put through it — so you can't throw everything you've got at somebody's skull without paying for it. Which sounds like mercy.

It isn't. What actually happens is the fights go longer. Nobody gets stopped clean, so you both stand there absorbing, and absorbing, for minutes, for tens of minutes, and the number of times your head gets accelerated and stopped goes up. Way up.
And it's the number that does it. Not the knockouts. The number.

I didn't know that yet. I want to be fair to myself for one paragraph and then I'll knock it off. On that Sunday, in Denny's garage, with the heater ticking and my face like a thumb, I did not know that. I knew bare was worse. I did not know how it was worse. There's a difference, and the difference is the only thing standing between me and being a man who did this on purpose from the start, and I'm going to hold onto it, because it's a thin fucking margin and it's all I've got. "Say something," Denny said. "Eight hundred." "Sean." "What."

"When Marge went," he said, and stopped, and started again, which he did, which was the only tell he had, "I painted the whole house. Inside and out. Took me five months. I painted rooms nobody'd been in since 1988. You understand what I'm telling you." "You're telling me to paint the house." "I'm telling you I know what a man does."
"Denny, if I painted that house I'd have to go in every room in it."

He didn't have anything for that. It's the only time I ever shut him up in thirty-four years and I'd give a lot to have it back, because after that he stopped saying it out loud and started just looking at me, and a man can argue with a sentence. "Second week of December," he said. "I'll wrap you." "You'll wrap me."
"I'll wrap you and I'll hold the fucking bucket and I'll tell you when you're loading the left, and that's the whole of my contribution to your life, apparently, so let me do it right."
5. Nine Seconds

The VFW in Cicero had a drop ceiling with a brown stain shaped like Ohio and a bar with a sign on it that said CASH ONLY — DON'T ASK, and the ring was a real ring, borrowed, with real ropes, and there was a woman selling raffle tickets for a smoker.
The kid's name was Andriy Kovalenko and he was twenty-six and he did not know how to fight and he could hit like the door of a car.

Round one I outboxed him. Left hand in his face, forty-one times, a jab is not a punch it's a ruler, it measures the distance and tells the right hand where to go, and I stuck it in his eye socket until his eye socket was a color. Round two I got greedy.

That's all it was. I want to make it sound like fate and it was greed. He dropped his right coming in and I saw the gap and I stepped in to put the left hook through it and I stepped in about four inches too far, and he threw a right hand blind, with his eyes half shut, not aiming at anything, the way a man swats at a wasp — and it landed on the hinge of my jaw.

There's a spot. Every fighter knows it and nobody explains it well, so here: the jaw is a lever, and it's hinged just under the ear, and if you hit the far end of that lever from the side, the head rotates. Not back. Around. And the brain, floating in its cup and a half of fluid, has to rotate too, except the outside of it starts rotating before the inside does, and all the long fibers running through it — the wiring, the millions of little cables that carry every single thing you are from one part of you to another — get twisted and stretched at once. Every one of them. Simultaneously.
The lights don't go out. That's television. What happens is the floor arrives.

I don't remember going down and I don't remember the count. Ruiz told me afterward that I got up at seven and that I looked at him and said Nuala, clearly, twice, and he waved it off, which was correct, and Denny came in and got me under the arms. Here's what I do remember.

I remember I was on the canvas on my right side with my cheek on it and the canvas smelled like a mat, that dead rubbery smell, and about a foot from my face there was a cigarette burn in it from some other decade, and I was looking at the burn. And then she was there.
I need to be careful here. This is the whole book. This is the thing I spent everything on, and if I fuck up the description of it then nothing after it makes any sense, so let me go slow.

She was not a picture. She was not a memory. I want to explain the difference and I don't think I can, but here it is: when you remember someone you are the one doing it. You're the projectionist. You're back in the booth running the reel and you know the whole time that you're in the booth. This was not that. There was no booth.

She was in the kitchen in Hegewisch, our kitchen, the one with the burner that clicks four times before it lights, and it was afternoon, and the light was coming in over the sink at the angle it comes in at around four o'clock in the fall, that low gold that gets into everything. She had her hair up in the elastic she kept on her wrist. She had the blue cardigan with the pilled elbows. She was standing at the counter doing something with her hands that I couldn't see and she turned partway around and she looked at me over her shoulder and she said, "Sean, did you move my keys?"

And I could smell her. That's the thing. That's the thing I could never make anybody understand afterward, and I stopped trying. I could smell her hair. There is no memory that has a smell in it. Memory is silent film with the smell burned off. This had everything. I said something. I don't know what.

She said, "Because they're not on the hook," and she made the face, the one where she pushed her tongue into her cheek, the one she made at me nine thousand times over four years about the keys, the keys, the fucking keys, and I hadn't seen that face since the fourth of November 2017 and I would have given both my hands and my eyes and my name to see it and there it was, there she was, breathing, four feet away, alive in a kitchen. It went on for about four minutes.

I know it was four minutes because Denny had me on the stool with an ice bag on my neck and he said afterward that I was gone for four minutes, sitting up, eyes open, not answering, and he was about ten seconds from calling an ambulance, and then I came back and looked at him and said, "Where'd she go?"
And Denny Fewster, who has known me since I was twelve, said: "Who?"
6. Therefore
Nine seconds.

That's how long I was on the floor. Seven-count plus the getting up. Nine seconds by the clock on the wall of a VFW hall in Cicero, Illinois, and in those nine seconds I had four minutes with my wife, which is a rate of exchange that I would like somebody to sit down and explain to me, and nobody ever has, and I have asked a neurologist.

Nobody saw anything. That's what I keep coming back to. Forty guys and a woman with a raffle book and not one of them saw a single thing worth mentioning. A middle-aged guy got dropped and got up. That was the event, out here, in the room. In here it was the fourth of November and the light was coming in over the sink and she was alive.

I finished the fight. Won the third on Ruiz's card and lost the decision, which was right, and Kovalenko's people were happy, and there was a moment where the kid hugged me and said something about how he'd watched me on a card at the UIC Pavilion when he was fourteen, and I said something back, and I have no idea what either of us said because I was not there. I was doing arithmetic.

I sat in my truck in the lot of a VFW in Cicero for fifty minutes with the engine off in December and I did arithmetic, and this is the part where a normal man goes to a grief group and I went to a spreadsheet. The facts as I had them:

One. It had never happened before. Four years, three hundred and something nights alone in that house, every photograph, every voicemail I couldn't delete, her coat still in the hall — nothing. Not once. Grief doesn't give you the person. That's the joke at the center of it that nobody warns you about. Grief gives you a hole shaped like the person, and you can walk around it and describe its edges in great detail for the rest of your life and you will never once get to see her face. Two. It happened tonight.

Three. Tonight was different from every other night of the last four years in exactly one respect, and the respect was that a twenty-six-year-old from Ukrainian Village had rotated my head about forty degrees around its own axis at eight hundred pounds of force. Four. Therefore.
I sat with the therefore for a long time. Long enough that the lot emptied out and a guy came and put a chain across the entrance and had to unlock it again to let me out, and gave me a look.
And I want to tell you that I was horrified. That I sat in that truck and understood what I was looking at and recoiled from it like a decent man.

I did not. I want to say that the thing I felt, sitting there with a jaw I couldn't fully close and blood in the pocket of my mouth, was closer to what a man feels when the tests come back and it isn't cancer. It was relief. Enormous, warm, obliterating relief. Because for four years the situation had been: she is gone and there is no way to her. And now the situation was: there's a way to her. It's expensive. Fine. Everything's expensive.

I drove home on Cicero Avenue with the window down because the cold felt good on the eye, and I put the radio on and it was some jingle for a mattress place, and I laughed so hard I had to pull over, and I could not have told you what was funny. I still can't. I've thought about it a lot. I think what was funny was: four years of therapy referrals I never called, and a bereavement group at St. Kevin's with folding chairs and a percolator, and a book my sister sent me about stages, and it turns out the answer was a Ukrainian roofer's kid with a lazy right hand.
You do have to laugh. Or you don't, but then what have you got.
7. The Honest Way
I tried to get it for free first. I want that in the record too.

For twelve days I tried to get it the honest way, the way you're supposed to, the way the pamphlet says, and I am here to report that the honest way is a fraud and the pamphlet is a fraud and whoever wrote it never lost anybody.

I got the photographs down out of the closet. There are four hundred and eleven photographs of Nuala Deane on this earth and I have all of them and I laid them out on the dining table in rows like a man doing a jigsaw of somebody's face, and I sat there under the overhead with a beer going warm and I looked at each one for a long time.

Here's what a photograph is. A photograph is a picture of a picture. You don't remember her, you remember the photo, and after enough years the photo has eaten the memory, quietly, the way ivy eats a wall, and what you're left with is a woman standing at Montrose Beach in 2014 in a green jacket, permanently, at that one angle, forever, and you cannot rotate her, and she has no smell, and she does not turn around.

I played the voicemail. There's one. Eleven seconds. She's in a Jewel and she wants to know if we have paprika. That's the whole thing, that's the last recording of my wife's voice on this earth, the word paprika, and I have listened to it enough times that I have destroyed it — not the file, the file's fine, but the listening. It's a sound now. It's just a sound my phone makes.

I went in the closet. Her side. I stood in there with the door shut and my face in the shoulder of the wool coat with the toggles, the one she wore to her mother's funeral, and I breathed in as deep as a man can breathe. Cedar block. Dry cleaning. Dust.
Four years is how long it takes. That's the number, if anybody wants it. Four years and the last of her is out of the wool.
And I sat on the floor of that closet, forty-four years old, with a face like a bag of plums, and I understood the shape of my situation with total clarity for the first time.

Everything I had left of her was representation. Photographs, recordings, objects, stories I'd told so many times they'd worn smooth like steps. All of it secondhand. All of it me, doing an impression.
Except for four minutes in a VFW hall in Cicero, where she had turned around and asked me about her keys, and I could smell her hair. That wasn't a representation. That was her.

I don't care what anybody says about that. I know what everybody says about that. I have since had it said to me by a woman with two degrees, kindly, in a room with a window, and she was right, and I don't care.

There is a version of this where I'm crazy. I've considered it at length, it's a real option, and I want to say for the record that I checked. I know what year it is. I know who I am. I paid my taxes in April, badly, but so does everybody. I am not a man who sees things.
I'm a man who saw one thing. Once. Under a specific and reproducible set of conditions.

And on day twelve I put the four hundred and eleven photographs back in the box and I put the box back in the closet and I closed the door, and I picked up the phone, and I sat with it in my hand for a while, doing nothing, the way you sit with a phone when you already know what you're going to do with it and you'd like the record to show a period of reflection.

There's a drawer in the sideboard in the dining room, the middle one, and in it are the things that came back to me in a plastic bag from the Illinois State Police in November of 2017, and a manila envelope from the funeral home, and some paperwork, and one other item, and I have not opened that drawer since the week after, and I open it in chapter twenty, and when I open it there's something in it that doesn't make sense.

I'm telling you it's there because I'm not a fucking magician. I don't want any credit for surprising you later. It's a drawer in a sideboard in a dining room in Hegewisch and it has been sitting there the entire time, twelve feet from where I sleep, and I walk past it every day of my life, and there is a piece of paper in it, and everything that happens to me in this book happens because I did not open a drawer.
9. A Guy With a Phone
"Sean Vardy," said Gaz Tunney, on the second ring. "The man himself. How's the face." "The face is fine." "I heard you got dropped." "I got dropped."
"Kovalenko's people are asking about a rematch, actually, if you want it, they'll do nine, they liked the crowd —" "Denny said you talked about bare."

There was a pause on the line about a second and a half long and I want to be precise about that pause because I have thought about it since. It was not a pause of reluctance. Gaz Tunney was not sitting there with his conscience. It was the pause of a man opening a different tab. "Bare," he said. "Yeah. Okay. Yeah, I can do bare." "When."

"January's when it picks up. There's a thing on the twenty-second, back of the transfer yard off Torrence, that's a truck bay, it's indoors, it's heated, sort of, there's a guy sells beer out of a cooler. That's a grand." "January's seven weeks." "It's the twenty-second." "That's seven weeks, Gaz." Another pause. Different one. "You in a hurry?"

And here is where I should have heard it. That's the sentence. If you want to find the exact place where I could have stepped off, that's it, that's the doorway, right there, a five-foot-six man in a quarter-zip with a phone in each hand asking me a perfectly reasonable administrative question. You in a hurry? "I could use the money," I said. "Sure," said Gaz.

Neither of us believed it and neither of us cared, and that was the entire nature of my relationship with Gaz Tunney for the next nine months. He never once asked me why. He never once told me to stop. He never once did anything but exactly what I asked him to do, promptly, with a confirming text, and it is very important to me that everybody understands that Gaz Tunney did not do this to me. I did this to me. I just needed a guy with a phone.

"There's a thing on the eighteenth of December," he said. "It's smaller. It's not really — look, it's a barn out past Beecher, it's a farm thing, it's forty guys and a generator. It's six hundred. It's bare." "Book it." "Sean, it's four days after you got knocked out." "Book it, Gaz." "Okay," said Gaz Tunney, and I heard him typing. "Booked."

I hung up and I stood in my kitchen in Hegewisch with the phone in my hand and the burner clicking four times before it lit, and I put the pan on, and I made two eggs, and I felt — and I'd like to be honest to the end here, because it's the only thing I've got left that's worth anything — I felt good.
I felt like a man who's found a doctor who'll write the script.
PART TWO: THE LEDGER
10. Nineteen Degrees

A pole barn nine miles past Beecher with a dirt floor and a diesel generator running two work lamps on stands, and it was nineteen degrees outside and about twenty-six inside, and you could see everybody's breath, forty of them, standing in a ring three deep, and the breath hung up in the rafters in a layer like weather.

No ropes. The ring was the men. That's it. That's what a bare fight is in a barn — the crowd is the ropes, and if you go back into them they push you forward, and they push hard, because they're drunk and it's their turn to be part of it.

No rounds. A count. When a man goes down the ref counts to twenty and if you're up you go again, and there is no minute on a stool, there is no corner, there is no water unless somebody hands it to you between counts. It goes until it stops.

The man's name was Errol Boyce and he was thirty-eight and he was a scaffolder out of Chicago Heights and he was the first genuinely dangerous person I fought in this whole run, and I have thought about him kindly ever since.
Let me tell you about hitting a man in the face with a bare hand.

The face is not soft. Everybody thinks the face is soft. The face is a bucket of bone with about four millimeters of skin over it, and the parts of it that stick out — the brow ridge, the cheekbone, the point of the chin, the top of the skull — are the hardest bone in the human body, harder than your femur, per square inch. Your hand is twenty-seven bones the size of pencils held together with string.

You hit a skull with a bare fist and one of two things happens. If you get it right, you land on the jaw or the temple with the two big knuckles, the index and the middle, driving straight through the wrist, and the force goes into the man and not into you. If you get it wrong — if you land a half-inch out, on the little-finger side, or you land on the top of his head because he's ducked — then the fifth metacarpal, the long thin bone behind your pinkie, snaps.

It doesn't hurt when it goes either. It just makes a noise you feel in your teeth, and afterward the knuckle is gone, there's a dent where a knuckle used to be, and the hand still works, mostly, in the way that a chair with three legs is still a chair if you're careful. I broke mine ninety seconds in.
I'd like to say I fought on out of courage. I fought on because the alternative was to go home to Baltimore Avenue on the eighteenth of December with a broken hand and nothing else.

So I fought with one hand for — I want to say twenty minutes and Denny says it was closer to thirty-five. I fought it on the back foot and I fought it with my forearms up in front of my face like a man carrying a stack of plates and I let Errol Boyce hit those forearms until my forearms didn't work either, and then I let him hit my head, because that's what was left.
Here's what he did to my face over the course of half an hour.
He closed the left eye first, which is a mercy, since the right one was still healing and now both sides of my head were rumor and I could stop worrying about seeing.

He split the left eyebrow, new cut, virgin skin, and a new cut in fresh skin bleeds worse than an old one — the old ones are half scar and scar has fewer vessels in it. So the blood came down that side in a sheet.

He broke my nose. That's the fourth time. When it goes you hear it inside your own head, a crunch like somebody stepping on a snail, and then instantly you can't breathe through it and the tears come — not crying, it's a plumbing thing, the nose and the eyes are connected and when the nose fills the eyes water — and you are now a man with two blind eyes and no air.

And somewhere in there he got me on the cheekbone with a straight right and I felt the zygomatic arch, which is the bone bridge you can feel running from just below your eye back to your ear — put two fingers on your own face and you're touching it now — I felt it give. Not break through. Depress, and come back. Like the roof of a car.

Somewhere around minute twenty-five I stopped being able to hold a thought in my head for longer than about a second and a half. That's the honest description. Not dizzy. Not dazed. There was simply no place to put anything. You'd start a sentence in your own mind and by the middle of it the beginning was gone, and the sentence would just stand there like a man who's walked into a room and forgotten why. And that's when it came.

She was in the kitchen. Same light, that four-o'clock gold over the sink. She had the cardigan on and her hair in the elastic and she was doing something with her hands at the counter and she turned around and she said:
"Sean, did you move my keys?" And I could smell her.

It was warm and it was complete and it went on for a long time, and out in the barn, according to Denny, I was on my knees in the dirt with my hands down and Errol Boyce was standing over me, and Errol Boyce — and this is why I've thought about him kindly ever since — Errol Boyce would not hit me. He stood there. He looked at the men and he said, out loud, to a barn full of drunks in Will County, "He's done, he's done, somebody get him." Nobody got me. They counted to twenty. She said, "Because they're not on the hook." She pushed her tongue into her cheek.

Two men picked me up under the arms and walked me out to Denny's Buick through the cold with my feet dragging tracks in the gravel, and I was smiling, apparently, with a face that had approximately no structural relationship to a face, and Denny Fewster said the only thing he said the whole way back to Hegewisch, which was: "That's it, then." And I said, "That's what?" And he said, "Nothing. That's nothing."
11. The Long Version
All right. Since we're going to be here a while, and since a man who won't tell you where he came from is usually hiding something dumber than a crime.

My father was Emmett Vardy and he worked at Wisconsin Steel on the East Side, in the eighty-inch mill, from 1961 until a quarter past three in the afternoon on the twenty-eighth of March, 1980, at which time a man came out onto the floor and told three thousand men to go home.

Not laid off. Closed. That afternoon. There was no notice and there were no severance checks and the paychecks they'd already handed out that week bounced, all of them, at every currency exchange from Torrence to Ewing, because the company had gone under between the printing and the cashing. Men stood in line at the Commercial Avenue exchange with paper in their hands that was worth exactly nothing, and the guy behind the glass had to say it three thousand times. My father was forty-one. I was three.

He got another job. I want to be fair to him. He got two. He drove for a linen service and he did nights at a warehouse in Riverdale, and he did that for about six years, and somewhere in the middle of those six years the actual Emmett Vardy left and did not tell anybody, and what was left came home and sat in the brown chair.

That's the whole of my childhood, if you want it in one image. A man in a brown chair in a front room on Baltimore Avenue with the television on and the sound down, and a boy on the floor, and neither of them saying anything, for years. He wasn't violent. I want to be clear, because everybody's waiting for that and it would be tidier. He never hit me once in his life. He just went out, like a pilot light, and stayed out, and the house got cold in a way that had nothing to do with the furnace.

My mother's name was Deirdre and she cleaned at the Hegewisch branch library and at two doctors' offices, and she is the only person in this story who did everything right and got nothing for it. She died in 2009 of something in her pancreas, quickly, which I understand is the good version.

In 1988 I was twelve and a kid named Ruben Salas told me there was a gym over on 106th where they let you in free, and I went, and it wasn't free, it was three dollars a month, and Denny Fewster paid it for me for four years and never once mentioned it, and I only found out in 2003 from somebody else. Here's why I stayed. Not the boxing. The building was warm.
That's it. That's the truth. The Ironbound gym on 106th had a boiler that worked and my house had a man in a chair, and I would have gone there to learn accounting.
But then there's the other thing, which took longer to notice.

In a fight, there is nothing else. There's no room in it. Whatever you are carrying — and I was twelve and I was already carrying, everybody's carrying by twelve — you cannot carry it and slip a jab at the same time. The head empties. It's the only place I have ever found where the head empties.
I want you to hold onto that, because it comes back in about a hundred pages and it's going to cost me my life.

Pro at twenty-five, which is late. Nineteen and four and one over nine years. I was never going to be anything and I knew it by the fourth fight, and I stayed anyway, because what else, and because for a few years there it paid better than the roof.

Twenty-thirteen: I fought a card at a casino in Elgin and afterward, in the lobby, a woman with a hospital badge still clipped to her bag looked at my face and said, "You know you're going to have to do something about that eye." Nuala Deane, thirty-four, a respiratory therapist at Christ, from Beverly, six brothers, a mouth on her like a dropped tray of cutlery. We were married in nine months.
I want to say something about her now, before everything, and I want you to remember I said it.

She was funny. Not funny for a woman, not funny for a nurse. Funny. She could do the whole of my family in voices. She once described my father's chair as "the only piece of furniture in Illinois with a hostage." She said things at funerals that made people run outside. When I say I miss her I am not talking about a soft warm presence in a kitchen. I am talking about a specific, mean, extremely fast intelligence that could take the roof off a room, and if you take nothing else from all this, take that, because a long way further on I'm going to show you a version of her that's soft and warm and vague in a kitchen and I need you to already suspect it.

Twenty-fifteen: the retina had already gone in 2010 — a fight in Hammond, a thumb, and then a month later a curtain coming down over the bottom of my vision like somebody drawing a blind, and a surgeon at
Christ with a laser, and you're done. And then in March of 2015 we had a son.

Fionn Emmett Vardy. Eight pounds one ounce. Born on a Wednesday at Christ, in the same building she worked in, delivered by people she'd eaten lunch with for twelve years, and he was perfect, and I held him and he had a hand like a little wet leaf.

He got sick on day seven. It was a bacteria that lives in about a quarter of all women, that does nothing to them, that is completely harmless right up until it isn't, and it went into his blood and from his blood into the lining around his brain, and they gave him everything they had, in the building where his mother worked, with everyone she knew standing over him.
He died on the twenty-second of March, 2015, at eleven days old, at four in the morning, and I want to say one thing about it and then I'm going to close this door. I did not cry.

Not at the hospital, not at the funeral home, not at the little grave at Holy Cross that costs less than a car. I stood next to my wife, who was making a sound I had never heard a human being make, and I put my hand on her back, and I felt absolutely nothing at all, and I have never told anybody that, and I want it written down.
I don't think I ever came back on. I think I went out like my father, in a chair, and it took eighteen months for anybody to notice.

That's what killed the marriage, by the way. Not Fionn. Fionn is what happened to us. What killed the marriage is what I did afterward, which was nothing, for three years, in a front room, with the sound down.
And then on the fourth of November 2017 my wife died on the Bishop Ford in the rain, at 11:53 at night, in a car, alone.
That's the long version. Or that's the version I had, on the eighteenth of December, driving home from a barn past Beecher with a hand in four pieces.
I want you to notice I got all the way through it without mentioning why she was on the expressway at that hour.

I got through it that way for four years. I got very good at it. I could tell you my whole life in ten minutes and go right past the hole in the middle of it like a man walking around a manhole he's stopped seeing.
12. Eleven Days

I said I was closing that door and then I drove home from Beecher with a hand in four pieces and couldn't sleep for it, so we're going to open it, and I'll be quick, and I'd appreciate it if nobody was kind to me about it afterward. Day one. The eleventh of March, 2015. Eight pounds one ounce. Christ, fourth floor, the building his mother had worked in for twelve years, delivered by a woman named Jolene who had eaten lunch with Nuala twice a week since 2006 and who cried handing him over, in the good way.
He had black hair, a lot of it, standing straight up like he'd had a fright. He had a hand like a little wet leaf and when I put my finger in it, it shut.

I'd like to say what that did to me and I can't, and that's not modesty, it's an engineering failure. There's no part on me for it. Day two. Home. Baltimore Avenue. The car seat took me thirty-five minutes and I have built roofs. Days three, four, five, six. Nothing. That's the whole entry and it's the best one. Four days of nothing. He fed, he slept, he made a noise like a small door, Nuala's sisters came in shifts and filled the freezer, and I sat up at three in the morning with him on my chest in the front room with the television on and the sound down — that room, that chair, I want you to notice — and it is the only time in my life the chair was a good place to be. Day seven. He wouldn't feed.

That's the whole warning you get. There's usually no fever with one that small; it often goes the other way, they go cold, and the signs are that he isn't feeding, he's floppy, he isn't making the noise.
Nuala had him in her arms at twenty past eight in the morning and she said, in a voice I had never heard out of her, flat and low and completely calm: "Sean. Get the keys."
She knew. She'd been doing that job for twelve years. She knew in the kitchen at twenty past eight, holding him, and she did not say one word about it in the car.
What it was. There's a bacteria called group B strep. About one woman in four carries it, all the time, in the ordinary course of being a person. It does nothing.
It has no symptoms. It is not a disease, it is not anybody's fault, and it does not mean one thing about anybody.

They test for it late in a pregnancy, around eight months, and if you're positive they run antibiotics through you during the delivery and that handles it, nearly always. Nuala tested negative. Negative on paper in January and carrying it in March, because it comes and goes, because the test is a photograph of one afternoon.
It got into him on the way out, through the ordinary business of being born. It sat there six days doing nothing.

Then it went into his blood, and out of his blood into the lining around his brain — a thin wrapper of tissue over it, like the skin inside an eggshell — and once it's in there the lining swells, and there is nowhere in a skull for a swelling to go.
That's it. That's the entire mechanism. That is what killed my son: pressure in a box. Days seven to ten. The unit.
Everything in there is beige and there is no time. No windows in the room he was in. There's a clock, and you stop being able to read it as a clock; it becomes a thing on a wall with hands.

He was in a plastic box on a shelf with a lid, warmed, with portholes in the side you put your arms through. A line in the back of his hand, taped to a little board so he couldn't bend it. A line in his scalp for a day, which they do, which is standard, which is a good vein for it, and which is the worst thing I have ever looked at, and I have since had my own eyebrow held open with a hook.
A tube down his throat and a strip of foam tape across his upper lip holding it. The tape was blue.
I could get two fingers through the porthole and touch his foot. That was the size of the contact. Two fingers on a foot three inches long.

And the sound — that's what I've got most of, actually, not pictures. A soft continuous beeping at a rate, and a hiss, and every so often an alarm going somewhere down the row that isn't yours. You learn in six hours to tell your alarm from everybody else's, the way a woman knows her own child's cry across a park.

Nuala did not go home. Not once, in four days. She slept in the chair. And she did the thing I think about more than anything else in this book, which is that she worked — she talked to those people as a colleague, in their language, she read the numbers off the screen herself, she asked about the antibiotic and the dose and whether they'd gone to the second agent, and when the consultant came round at seven in the morning she stood up and had a conversation with him I could not follow one word of. She was fighting for him with the only hands she had. And I stood against the wall.

That's what I did. Four days. In writing: I stood against the wall by the sanitizer dispenser with my hands in my pockets and said "yeah" to people, and fetched coffee nobody drank, and once went out and moved the truck. Day ten, evening. The consultant took us into a small room.

There is always a small room. Every hospital on earth has it and it is the same room and there is a box of tissues on a low table and the box is always nearly empty, which I have never understood, because you'd think that's the one box in the building they'd stay on top of.
He said the swelling had done what swelling does. He said the scans showed damage in areas that don't come back. He said even in the best case.

He was a decent man, he did it properly, and he did not use one word we had to look up. I have no complaint against anybody who works in that building. I have exactly one complaint and it isn't with them. Day eleven. The twenty-second of March, 2015. Four in the morning.

They take the tube out and put a blanket round him and hand him to you. That's how it's done, and it's right, and it is also the cruellest arrangement human beings have ever devised — because the only time I held my son in that building after day seven was while he was dying in my arms.
Eleven days old. He weighed less leaving that room than he did going into it.

Nuala made a sound. I have heard men make noises with broken bones in them and I have never heard anything like it, before or since. It went on and it did not stop and a nurse came and stood in the doorway and did not come in.
And I sat on a plastic chair with my dead son on me and put my hand on my wife's back. And I felt nothing.
I have to be precise here, because it is the single most important fact about me and I have never once got it accurate.

It was not numbness. Numb is a thing you feel — you can report on numb, numb has a texture. It was not shock, and it was not denial, and it was not being strong for her, which is what two people have offered me over the years and which I could hit them for. It was that the room went administrative.
I looked at my wife and thought: she'll need water. I thought: somebody has to call Bernie. I thought: the truck's in short-stay and it's been eleven hours. I thought about the parking.
I sat there with an eleven-day-old boy going cold against my shirt and a fully functioning part of me was working the parking.
And underneath that there was a large flat calm place with nothing on it, and I have been standing on it ever since, and I did not put it there and I do not know the way off.

They gave us a memory box. It's a real thing they do and it's kind and I want that said. A card with his footprints in ink. The hat. A photograph. It's upstairs. Second bedroom at the back. On the shelf. I have not opened it.
Seven years. Twelve feet above the room where I sleep, in a house where I use four rooms out of eleven, there is a cardboard box with my son's feet in it.

And I want you to hold that up against what you already know I did — twenty-two months and every bone in my face, buying four-minute visits with a woman who was already gone — and notice that I never once, not for a single second, in any barn or scrap yard or truck bay or in a room three hundred feet under this city, tried to buy one with him. I don't have an explanation. I've looked for one.
The nearest I have got is this: I could not have stood it if it had worked.
13. The Tour

Recovery, second entry. Christmas week. Let's do the tour. The hand. Fifth metacarpal, left, snapped and displaced, which means the two ends had gone past each other and the knuckle had sunk into the back of my hand like a key pressed into dough. There is a dent there now, permanently, and when I make a fist the little finger sits a quarter inch lower than it used to and points slightly at my thumb, as if it's about to make a suggestion.

I did not go to an emergency room, because an emergency room asks how, and I did what men in this line of work do, which is I let Denny pull it — he took the finger and pulled straight and steady for about six seconds while I said several things about his mother — and then he buddy-taped it to the ring finger with a bit of gauze between so the skin wouldn't rot, and that was the treatment. That's the whole treatment. It healed crooked and it healed strong and it aches at about forty degrees Fahrenheit, which in this city is most of the year. The nose. Broken and pushed slightly to the left, so that I now breathe about seventy percent on one side and thirty on the other, and when I lie on my back I make a sound like a coffee maker finishing.

Also: septal hematoma. Which sounds fancy and means blood collected between the wall of cartilage in the middle of your nose and the skin covering it, and if you leave it there the cartilage starves — same principle as the ear, the cartilage gets fed through the skin lying on it — and the whole bridge of your nose collapses into your face like a tent with the pole out. Denny drained it on the twentieth of December in the bathroom of his two-flat with a syringe and a needle he flamed with a lighter, and I sat on the edge of the tub, and it made a sound like a straw at the bottom of a milkshake, and about twenty milliliters of my own blood came out into a paper cup, and we both looked at it. "Merry Christmas," Denny said. The face, generally. Both eyes shut for four days. Not swollen — shut, so that I had to hold the lid open with two fingers to see the sink. The left cheek stayed numb for nine weeks, from the eye down to the corner of the mouth, because there's a nerve that comes out through a little hole under the eye socket and delivers sensation to that whole quadrant of your face, and something had sat on it. When it came back it came back as pins and needles, but on the outside of my face, which is a thing I do not recommend.

Bruising went black at day two, purple at four, a real theatrical green at seven, and yellow at ten, and the yellow is the worst because yellow is when people ask. The forearms. Both. Wrist to elbow. Solid bruise, front and back, with two lumps on the left ulna — the bone on the little-finger side of your forearm, the one you can feel the whole length of — where he'd hit the same spot enough times to make the bone lay down extra material. That's a real thing. Bone remodels where it gets hit. Old bare-knuckle men had forearms like axe handles and it wasn't muscle. Work. Ostrowski does not roof in January so that was moot. Christmas. My sister Colleen called from Naperville on the twenty-fourth and I told her I'd been in a car thing, and she said, "Another one?" and I said, "It's a bad intersection," and she said nothing for four seconds and then talked about her kids for twenty minutes, and I said the right things in the right gaps, and we hung up loving each other exactly as much as before, which is not nothing. The head. Now here's the part.

For twelve days after Beecher I could not remember what I had eaten. Any day. I'd stand in the kitchen at seven at night and genuinely not know whether I'd had food since waking, and the only way to find out was to look in the trash. I put my keys in the refrigerator on the twenty-third — and yes, I know, the keys, I heard it too, I stood there with the fridge open and laughed until I had to sit down on the floor.
I had a headache the whole twelve days that lived behind the left eye and had a taste, which is not a thing headaches are supposed to have.

And I could not find a single word I wanted. Not big ones. I lost spatula for six minutes. I stood in my own kitchen holding it, saying "the — the — the flat fucking thing," out loud, alone, to nobody.

And in the middle of that, on Christmas Day, sitting in the front room with the television on and the sound down, in the chair, in the chair, I noticed that I had done a piece of arithmetic without deciding to.
Beecher had taken me about thirty-five minutes and something on the order of two hundred punches to get four minutes of my wife.
Cicero had taken nine seconds and one punch to get the same four minutes.
I sat there in my father's position with a hand taped to itself and I did not think that's a hundred and twenty times worse. I thought: it's still cheap.
14. The Trade
Denny Fewster's tackle box.

I want a chapter on it because nobody knows this trade anymore. There are maybe two hundred men alive who can actually do it, and in twenty years there'll be none, and it is the most obscene and most tender thing one human being does for another for money.

It's a green Plano box, three trays, from a sporting goods place on Torrence that shut in 2004. Here's what's in it. The enswell. A chunk of stainless the size of a matchbox with a handle on it, and it lives in the ice bucket all night so it comes out at about thirty-four degrees. You press the flat of it — press, never rub; rubbing tears the tissue under the skin and doubles the swelling — into the puffed area, hard, and hold. What you are doing is squeezing the fluid out sideways and shutting the small vessels down with cold so less arrives. You get thirty seconds between rounds and about eleven of them are the enswell. Adrenaline, one in a thousand. A little brown bottle. Adrenaline clamps blood vessels shut, so a swab of it pushed hard into a cut will stop a bleed that nothing else will stop. That bottle is the whole trade. The old men soaked the swab and then squeezed it out so it wasn't dripping, because if it runs into the eye you have blinded your own fighter, and every cutman has done that once and remembers it forever. Thrombin powder. Makes blood clot on contact. Goes into a deep one you can't close. Petroleum jelly, in a tin, worked soft. Once you've stopped it, you seal it — a sealed cut is a slippery cut, and the next punch goes off it instead of into it. Swabs, gauze, tape, a curved hemostat — locking pliers the size of a pen, for grabbing something inside a wound. A scalpel. Number eleven blade. That one needs explaining.

When an eye swells shut it is not swollen with air. It's a sac of blood under the skin: the lid has filled, there's nowhere for it to go, and it has closed the eye like a garage door. Ice will not move that inside a minute. So what a real cutman does, and what almost nobody will do now, is open it. He takes the blade and makes a small cut in the puffed lid along the natural line and lets the blood out.

It's been done to me twice. The second time was Hammond, 2007, and Denny came into the corner and said, "Look at me," and I looked at him, and he did it, and it took under four seconds, and I saw the rest of the fight, and I won it.
He was never licensed to do that. Nobody is. He did it because otherwise the fight gets stopped and the man doesn't get paid.

Think about that properly. A man kneeling in front of you in thirty seconds of quiet in a very loud room, holding your face still with his left hand, thumb on the cheekbone, cutting you with his right — so that you can go back out and be hit some more.
That's love, in the trade I was in. That is exactly what it looks like. It doesn't look like anything else and it never once gets called by its name. What Vic had. A headlamp and superglue.

That's not fair to Vic. Vic had a box too and Vic was competent and Vic had no choice about the glue, because there are no rounds down there — so there is no thirty seconds, so there is no repair. There's only afterward, on a wet floor, with a hundred and forty men going up the drift and a generator winding down.

Superglue on a face. Everybody does it and everybody knows better. The medical version is a slightly different molecule that doesn't heat up as much when it sets; the hardware-store version gets genuinely hot in the wound and kills a thin layer of tissue as it cures. It holds. It holds beautifully. And underneath, the edges have been cooked, so they never knit, and the scar comes out wide and stupid with no strength in it, and the next punch opens it wider than the first one did.
Denny told me that on a step in August and I let a man's brother-in-law do it to me in January anyway.

And then the thing about a face. Here's what nobody says out loud. A cutman's entire job — the box, the ice, the adrenaline, the blade, thirty years of skill — is not to heal anybody. Nothing in that box heals anything. It is a kit for deferring damage by a few minutes so that more damage can be done.
He isn't a doctor. He's the man who keeps the machine running past the point where the machine is asking to stop.

And they are, to a man, the kindest people in the sport. That's not a paradox, it's just what the job does. You spend forty years with your thumb on the cheekbones of frightened men, closing them so they can go and be opened, and either you go hard as a nail or you go entirely the other way — and the ones who go the other way stay in it, and the hard ones leave, because the hard ones can't stand how sad it is. Denny went the other way somewhere around 1979.
And in August he stood on my step in a windbreaker and told me he wasn't doing it anymore, and I told him he was just a man who watched.

I have had a lot of time to work out which of us in that arrangement was the doctor and which was the one keeping the machine running past the point where it was asking to stop. It isn't a close call. It never was.
15. The Failed Purchase
January twenty-second, the truck bay behind the transfer yard off Torrence.

Concrete floor, forty feet of it between the roll-up doors, salt tracked in from the lot and dried in white maps. Two propane heaters roaring at the ceiling doing absolutely nothing at floor level. Sixty men. A guy selling Old Style out of a cooler for four dollars and giving change out of a coffee can. Somebody's dog.

His name was Petey Sowa, he was thirty-five, he had a good beard and no chin under it, and I want to state clearly and in advance that I beat Petey Sowa comprehensively and that it was the worst night of my life to date. Because nothing happened.

I hit him with everything I had — the good hand, mostly, the right, because the left was twelve days out of tape and I couldn't close it past halfway. I broke his orbital floor in the twelfth minute, which is the thin plate of bone at the bottom of the eye socket, thin as a fingernail, thinner, and when it goes the eye can actually sink down into the gap and the man sees two of everything on the way up. I know I broke it because Petey Sowa afterward could not look at the ceiling. He'd tip his head back and his eyes would stop tracking each other and one would drift and he'd say, "Huh."

And he hit me. Plenty. He caught me on the ear, twice, on the temple, four or five times, on the top of the head when I ducked in, which broke his hand, and on the mouth, which pushed my upper lip into my teeth and opened it on the inside, and a lip cut from the inside bleeds like a scandal.
And it went twenty minutes and I won it and I got up off the concrete twice and got up both times inside the count. And I did not get her.

I have to try to explain this and I don't think I'm going to manage it. Imagine you have a wife who is dead and you have found the one door in the world she is behind, and you have paid the toll at that door twice and gone through twice, and on the third time you pay the toll — you pay it in full, you pay double, you pay in bone — and you walk through the door and it's the truck bay behind a transfer yard off Torrence Avenue with sixty men shouting and a dog barking and a guy giving change out of a coffee can.
I stood in the middle of that floor with a thousand dollars coming and the crowd making the noise and I thought, quite calmly: Not enough.

Denny was in front of me with the bucket saying my name. There was blood coming out of my mouth in ropes and I let it. I was looking past him at the roll-up door. "It wasn't enough," I said. "What wasn't." "It has to be more."
Denny Fewster stood there with a bucket in a truck bay in January and looked at me for a long moment and then he said, "Sean. What has to be more?"
And here's the thing, here's the exact thing, here's the moment I'd point to if a judge asked me when I knew: I didn't tell him.

I had a chance, right there, to say a sentence out loud to another human being. Denny, when I get hit hard enough I see my wife. Eleven words. That's all it would have taken and it would have been over, because Denny would have driven me straight to Christ that night and sat in the waiting room until somebody looked at me, and I'd have been a man with a diagnosis in January instead of what I turned into.
I didn't say it because I knew — I knew, standing there, bleeding out of my mouth — that if I said it out loud, somebody would take it off me. So I said: "The money."
And Denny said, "Right," and put the towel on my head, and that was that.

That's how you do it, incidentally. That's the mechanism. People think there's a moment where you decide to destroy yourself and it's dramatic and you're on a bridge somewhere. There isn't. There's a moment where somebody who loves you asks you a direct question in a truck bay and you tell them a small lie about money, and everything after that is just scheduling.
16. Permission
I went to Christ in February and I told myself it was about the numbness.

That's what I said at the desk and that's what I said to the resident and it was even half true — nine weeks of a dead left cheek will get a man into a building. But you don't drive forty minutes to the hospital where your wife worked, and where your son died, and sit in that lobby under that specific ceiling, for a numb face. You do that when some part of you has raised its hand.
They sent me to neurology because of the history. That's a word they use for a man who has been hit in the head professionally for twenty-two years. History.

Dr. Parvaneh Ashkani was maybe fifty, small, with reading glasses pushed up into her hair and a South Side accent laid over something older, and she looked at my chart for a long time before she looked at me, which I appreciated, because everybody looks at the face first and then pretends they didn't. "Sean Vardy," she said. "Nineteen and four and one." "You looked me up."

"My brother took me to the Aragon in 2006. You fought a Puerto Rican kid, you got outboxed for eight rounds and then you knocked him out with a left hook, and my brother stood on his chair." She took the glasses out of her hair. "It was very stupid and I've never forgotten it." "That's the review, generally."

She went through the face. Pressed under the eye socket, all around the rim, along the arch, made me clench my jaw with her fingers on the hinge, shone a light into both eyes for a long time, made me follow a pen, made me push against her hand.

Then she sat down and asked me about the last twelve months and I lied, and she let me, and then she asked me a different way, and I lied worse. "How many," she said. "How many what." "Fights. Since the retina." "Four," I said.
She wrote 4 on the paper and put a little mark next to it that I have thought about a great deal since, because I'm fairly sure the mark meant no.
"Here's what I want to tell you," she said, "and I want you to actually listen, because everybody in your line of work has heard a version of it and stopped hearing it around 1996.

"Forget knockouts. Knockouts are what got measured because knockouts are what people notice. They're not the dose. The damage tracks the total number of impacts. Every time your head gets accelerated and stopped. Sparring counts. Bag work counts, a little. The four hundred jabs you took in a gym in 1994 count. It's not the one that puts you down. It's the nine hundred that didn't." "That's a lot of nine hundreds." "Twenty-two years," she said. "Yes." And then she told me about the umbrella.

"Inside every nerve fiber in your head there are struts. Little rods running the length of it, holding it open, like the ribs inside an umbrella. There's a protein that clips onto those rods and keeps them stable. When the head gets shaken, hard, a lot, that protein comes loose. And once it's loose it clumps. And once it clumps it doesn't clear — the clumps sit there and they spread, cell to cell, outward. And they start in a very particular place, which is down in the folds of the brain where the blood vessels run, because that's where the shaking is worst." "Can you see it? On a scan?"
"No," she said. "Not in a living person. Not yet. We can only find it afterward." "So what do I do." "You stop," said Parvaneh Ashkani.

I sat there in a paper gown in a room with a window and I thought about how to ask what I'd come to ask without asking it, and eventually I did the thing everybody does, which is I put it on a friend.

"Doc. A guy I know. He got knocked out, and he — he saw his wife. She's dead. He saw her. Not remembered her. Saw her. Smelled her hair." She didn't look surprised, which surprised me. "How long ago did his wife die?" "Four years."

"Then his wife has been dead four years and he's a widower," she said, "and this is the most ordinary thing in the world, and nobody tells anybody, and it's a scandal that nobody tells anybody. Somewhere between a third and a half of bereaved people see or hear the dead. Half. Voices in the house, footsteps, the person sitting in a chair. It's not psychosis, it's not a breakdown, it isn't even considered a disorder. It's what a grieving brain does. It's so common that the strange thing is going four years without it." And there it was.

I want to freeze the frame here, because this is the single most important moment in my life, and it looks like nothing. A doctor being kind and being right. Every word she said was true. She was answering the question I actually asked her. She had no way of knowing there was a second question underneath it, because I had specifically constructed the first one to make sure she couldn't see it. "So it's normal," I said. "It's very normal." "It's not the head injury."
Parvaneh Ashkani paused. I have replayed that pause maybe four hundred times.

"Grief can do it on its own," she said. "A brain injury can also do it. Damage in the memory regions can produce something that isn't a recollection — it's an event. Present tense. Full sound and smell. There was a surgeon in the nineteen-thirties who touched an electrode to the side of a woman's brain during an operation and she heard a song playing, in a room, from thirty years before. Not remembered it. Heard it." "So it could be either."
"It could be either. It doesn't matter which, Mr. Vardy, because the answer to both of them is the same, and the answer is that you stop fighting."

She was wrong about that one thing and only that one thing, and it was the thing that killed me. It mattered enormously which. Because if it was grief, then it was free, and it would come again on its own, in a chair, in a house, some evening, for nothing. And if it was the head, it had a price.
I drove home on the Bishop Ford — which I do, which I have to, because it's the road — and I felt so light I had the window down in
February.
Grief hallucinations. A third to a half. Very normal. Nothing to do with the head at all. I had permission.

She'd given me four more fights and it took me about twenty minutes to spend the first of them, and she has never once in her life had a bad thought about that conversation, because I never told her, and I'm not going to, and that's my last decent act, keeping it off her.
17. Headlights
March. Fight five. A scrap yard in Riverdale, outdoors, half past four in the morning, because that's when the yard is empty and the gate guy is a cousin.

Twenty-eight degrees. They'd cleared a floor between two mountains of crushed sedans and lit it with the headlights of six cars pointed inward, and I want to say something about fighting in headlights, because it is the single most disorienting condition I have ever worked in and nobody warns you.

Six light sources at chest height, all pointed at the middle. So every man on that floor has three or four shadows going off him in different directions like a hand of cards fanned out. When the other fellow moves, four black versions of him move too, at four different speeds, on the ground and up the wall of crushed cars behind him. Your eye is built to track one thing. It does not know what to do with a man who arrives with an entourage.

And the beams are level with your face, so half the time you are looking directly into one and the other man is a silhouette with no features at all, no eyes to read, and reading eyes is about forty percent of what I know how to do.

His name was Dessie Pike, he was forty-one, and he was an actual professional in the sense that this was his living. Seventy-odd of these. A nose you could hang a coat on and ears like two pieces of dried fruit. Minutes one to six. He taught me something.

Pike did not throw at my head for the first six minutes. Not once. He worked the body exclusively, both hands, from close, and he did it the way a man loads a truck — no emotion in it at all, just placement. Left to the short ribs. Right under the elbow. Left again, same spot.

Body work in a bare fight is the smart play and almost nobody has the patience for it, because there's no drama and the crowd hates it. But a rib doesn't heal in a night and a head sometimes does, and a man who can't breathe can't hold his hands up in minute fifteen. Pike was thirty minutes ahead of me the whole time. Minutes six to eleven. I got greedy again, which is apparently my entire biography.

He'd been going downstairs so consistently that I started dropping my right elbow to cover, and at six forty he put a left hook over the top of it into the side of my head, right on the ear, and the ear went instantly hot and thick — the cartilage lifting off the skin, blood filling the gap, the whole thing swelling into a shape that is not an ear — and the world on that side turned into a seashell. That's the actual sensation. Not deafness. A roar, like a shell held to your head, permanent, with a fight going on inside it. Minute eleven. The rib.

Left hook to the body, and not the liver — the other side, low, the floating ribs. There are two down there at the bottom of the cage, the eleventh and the twelfth, and they are called floating because the front ends aren't attached to anything. They just end. Which means there is nothing to brace them and nothing to spread the load, and a good hook lands on a bone that is, structurally speaking, a stick lying loose in meat.
I felt it go. Not heard — felt, a sort of dull click deep in, and then a sensation of something being out of place that I have never had from any other bone.

And it does not put you down. That's the joke of a floating rib. It doesn't stop you at all. What it does is arrange that from that moment on, every single breath you take for six weeks arrives with an invoice attached, and a man breathes about eighteen times a minute, and I did the arithmetic on that in the truck afterward because I do the arithmetic on everything, and it came to somewhere around four hundred and fifty thousand. Minutes eleven to fourteen. He put me down twice.

First one I went to a knee and got up on the count of six. Second one I went over backward onto packed dirt with a piece of glass in it and I got up at twelve, and there is a photograph of that somewhere on somebody's phone, and I have never wanted to see it. Minutes fourteen to eighteen. And then I got him.

Right hand on the temple, over a lazy jab, with about four minutes left. It was the best punch I threw in the entire twenty-two months and it landed on the flat spot in front of the ear on a man who had seventy of these, and Dessie Pike went down on one knee and shook his head like a dog with water in its ear.
