The men in the headlights made the noise. That noise. In a scrap yard at ten to five in the morning in March, forty men with their breath going up into the beams, making the noise a crowd makes when something has gone wrong in front of them and they are glad.

He got up. Of course he got up. And we finished it standing, both of us, four minutes, neither man able to hurt the other anymore, just leaning and swinging, and they called it a draw because nobody had a coin.
VISIT THREE.
Not in the fight. Afterward — in the car, engine running, heater on, Denny gone off to piss behind a stack of doors.

That was new. Every previous one had come inside a minute of going down, on a floor, with a man's face over me. This one came twenty-five minutes later, sitting up, in a parked Buick, with the vents going.
I noted it. I filed it. I did nothing about it. That's a sentence I could put under a photograph of my own head.
The kitchen. The four o'clock light. The cardigan, the elastic, the counter. Sean, did you move my keys?
Three minutes and change, warm, complete. I could smell her hair over the smell of the heater.
And I answered her. I know I answered her out loud because Denny came back and caught the tail of it through the window.
I said: "They're in your bag, love. They're always in your bag."
Denny got in, and shut the door, and put his seatbelt on, and did not say anything for about a mile and a half. Then he said: "Who's in your bag?" And I said, "Nothing. Nobody. Drive."
18. A Following
Three weeks later, back in the truck bay off Torrence, and by now they knew me there.
That's a thing I should mention before this one, because it becomes load-bearing.

I had a following. By April. Not a large one and not a good one, but sixty men in a truck bay is a small enough world that an old pro with a wrecked face who never goes down easy becomes a fixture, and men would come up before and shake my hand and tell me they'd seen me at the Aragon, or on television at four in the morning on some Spanish channel in 2007. One fellow brought a program to sign. An actual program, from the UIC Pavilion, kept in a drawer for fifteen years, and I signed it on the hood of a car with a hand I could not fully close. They liked me because I stood there.

That's the whole of it. They did not like me because I could box, because by April I couldn't. They liked me because I would take an enormous amount and remain upright and they had never seen anybody do that in person.
And they had no idea — not one of them, ever — that standing there was not courage and was not stubbornness and was not some old fighter's pride.

It was the product. It was the actual thing I was in that building to purchase. They were watching a man shop. Fight six. A kid named Terrence Dawes, twenty-nine years old, ten pounds heavier than me, and fast in the way that only stops being a problem when a man is fifty. Minutes one to twelve. He took me apart with a jab.

I want to spend a paragraph on that, because everybody thinks a jab is a nothing punch, a range-finder, a thing you do while you're deciding. A jab thrown properly by a fast twenty-nine-year-old with no glove on his hand is a knuckle arriving at your face at about twenty miles an hour with a shoulder behind it, and the sensation is not being punched at all. It's being flicked in the face by a bus door. Sharp, flat, and it snaps your head back four inches and puts water in your eyes, and he did it a hundred and something times in twelve minutes, and every single one of them accelerated my head and stopped it, and every single one of them went on Ashkani's total.

He reopened both brows in the first four minutes. The left one from Beecher, the right one from the Golden Steer and six times before that. Both went in the same minute, one from a jab and one from a hook, and after that the entire fight became a blood management problem.

Here's blood management in a truck bay. There are counts but no rounds, so between counts you tip your head all the way back — which sends it down your throat, which is its own difficulty — and Denny gets in there with a cold sponge and clears the eye sockets, and you get maybe four seconds of vision back before it fills again. Your whole tactical world shrinks to how long since the last sponge. Minutes twelve to fifteen. Right eye gone entirely. Nose packed with clot and useless, so mouth-breathing only, which in a fight is a disaster — an open mouth is a broken jaw waiting for an appointment, and every fighter alive knows it and nobody can do a thing about it when the nose is shut.

And the cheek. I had been clenching so hard for fifteen minutes that I'd chewed the inside of my own left cheek to pieces, and there was a flap of it hanging loose in there, and my tongue kept finding it and would not leave it alone. It felt like a wet stamp. That's the detail I'd take out of the whole book if I could — not the brows, not the rib. The wet stamp. Minutes fifteen to nineteen. He hunted the chin and I let him look for it, and I want to be honest that this is the fight where I stopped fighting.

Not the next one, where I did it deliberately and made a whole thing of it. This one. Somewhere around minute sixteen against Terrence Dawes I quietly stopped trying to win and started trying to last, which are opposite skills, and the crowd could not tell the difference, and Denny could. Minute nineteen. He hit me on the point of the chin.

The point of the chin is the far end of the lever. Everything I said about the hinge and the rotation, doubled. My legs went before my head did — that's the order, the legs know first — and I went down on my back on the concrete of a truck bay with my arms out to the sides like a man making a snow angel.
VISIT FOUR.
The kitchen. Four o'clock. The cardigan. Her hair in the elastic. All of it exactly right, and warm, and complete. She turned around.
She said: "Sean, did you move my keys? Because they're not on the hook. Anyway." And then it stopped.
19. Anyway
Anyway.

I want to tell you about the word anyway and I want you to bear with me, because it's going to sound like the smallest thing in this entire book and it is the exact place where the floor went. Nuala Deane did not say anyway.

I don't mean she never used the word. I mean it wasn't in her rhythm. She was a fast talker from a family of eight and she went sideways constantly, and the way she got out of a sideways bit was by landing on you — she'd finish with a name, Sean, or a swear, or a question, or the tongue in the cheek. She closed on you. Anyway is what you say when you're getting yourself out of a room. It's a nothing word. It's a word for a woman at a bus stop with someone she doesn't know well.
It was flat, too. That's the other thing. The whole sentence came out on one level. Nuala's sentences went up in the middle.

I lay on the concrete in a truck bay off Torrence Avenue and Denny Fewster's face came into the top of my vision upside down and behind him were the ceiling and the propane heaters, and my first thought — my first thought, before am I hurt, before did I win, before anything — was: That wasn't right.

And my second thought, arriving before I was even sitting up, was the sound of my own voice explaining it to me. It's the venue. It's noisy in here, there's sixty guys, there's a dog. You got hit on the chin and the chin is a bad one, it rotates you, it's a rough delivery, of course the signal's degraded. It's like a bad phone line. The person on the other end is fine, Sean. The person on the other end is fine, it's the line.
And I lay there on cold concrete with my own blood running into my ear and I bought that. Wholesale. Immediately. No haggling.
Here's what I know now about that moment, and it's the only thing I actually learned from all of this, so I'll hand it over free:

You do not get warned once. You get warned every single time, clearly, in plain language, by something inside you that has no interest in your comfort and no talent for lying. And what happens is not that you miss the warning. You hear the warning, and then a second voice comes in immediately behind it — fast, fluent, reasonable, full of technical detail — and explains why the warning doesn't apply in your particular case.

That second voice is not you thinking. That second voice is the addiction talking, and the tell, the absolute tell, is that it's the only voice in your head that's ever prepared. It's got the explanation ready before you've finished having the doubt. Nothing honest is ever that fast.
I got up. I lost the decision. I took eight hundred dollars in an envelope with the flap tucked in.

And on the way to the car I found that I had gone from she said something wrong to it's the room to a third position entirely, which had assembled itself somewhere between the concrete and the door, and which was this: The signal's degrading because the connection isn't strong enough. I need to hit harder. I need to get hit harder. I need a cleaner line.
You see how that works? You see the beauty of it? The evidence that the thing is killing me had been converted, in under four minutes, without conscious effort, into a reason to do more of it.
I would like to meet the part of my brain that did that. I'd like to shake its hand. It's the most talented thing I have ever owned and it has never once worked in my favor.
20. The Middle Drawer

The rib made me sleep sitting up, and a man who sleeps sitting up in a front room at three in the morning eventually gets up and walks around his own house, and that's how I ended up in front of the sideboard on a Tuesday in April with a bag of frozen peas held against my side. The middle drawer. Four and a half years.
I'd like to describe opening it as some kind of decision. It wasn't. I opened it the way you open a drawer.

Contents. One clear plastic bag, sealed, with a red-and-white printed strip across the top and a case number written on in ballpoint. Inside: a phone with a cracked screen. A wedding band. A pair of glasses with one arm bent out at an angle that made my stomach turn over harder than any of the rest of it, because a bent arm on a pair of glasses is a velocity, it's the only object in there that tells you the speed. A hair elastic. Twelve dollars. And her keys.

One manila envelope from Zaremba & Sons with a death certificate and two carbons and an itemized invoice, and I want to note that the invoice for burying my wife had a line on it that said MISC. — $180.00, and that I have never found out what the misc was, and that for a while in 2018 I thought about it more than I thought about her.
One folded sheet, printed, three pages, stapled: ILLINOIS STATE
POLICE — VEHICLE CONTENTS INVENTORY.

And I sat down on the floor of my dining room with my back against the sideboard and my ribs screaming and I read it, and it went like this: Front passenger seat: one (1) handbag, brown leather, contents inventoried separately. Front passenger footwell: one (1) travel mug, stainless. Rear seat: one (1) suitcase, hardshell, blue, approx. 26 in. Rear seat: one (1) duffel bag, canvas, olive. Rear footwell: one (1) box, cardboard, containing books and framed photographs. Trunk: one (1) garment bag, black. Trunk: one (1) plastic tote, containing kitchen items. I read it four times.
Now here's what happens next, and this is the part I don't know how to make anybody believe, and I've stopped trying with the two people I've told, both of whom made a face. Nothing happened.

I read that inventory four times at three in the morning in April of 2022 — a suitcase, a duffel, a garment bag, a box with her books and her photographs in it, a tote of kitchen things — and my mind went smoothly and immediately to a place that had clearly been built and stocked and maintained for years in preparation for exactly this moment, and the place said: She was taking stuff to her sister's. Bernie was moving. She was helping Bernie move. And I thought: right. Bernie's move. That's right. Bernie moved in 2019.

I knew that. I've been to that condo. I helped carry a couch up two flights in 2019 with a bad shoulder and Bernie's husband complaining about his knee, and on the fourth of November 2017 Bernadette Deane was living in the same apartment in Mount Greenwood she'd been in for nine years and would stay in for two more.

I knew that on the floor of my dining room in April 2022 and I thought Bernie's move anyway, and I folded the sheet along the same creases, and I put it back in the drawer, and I closed the drawer, and I went and sat on the couch and put the television on with the sound down.
I want to be extremely careful about how I describe this, because it's the single strangest thing my own head ever did to me, stranger than any of the visits.

It was not denial in the way people mean it. I did not look at the evidence and refuse it. I looked at the evidence and there was a story already there, waiting, fully formed, that took the evidence in and dissolved it without a sound, the way the stomach handles food. Three seconds. No effort. No discomfort at all. Not the smallest flicker of hang on.
That story had been built by somebody. Somebody in there had been working on it, quietly, on my behalf, for four and a half years, keeping the house standing.
And I'd like to say I found out who, and had a word with him. But you'll notice I keep saying I like there's one of me.
21. The Ninth of November

I put the inventory sheet back in the drawer and closed it and went and sat on the couch, and that should have been the end of it, and it wasn't, because a thing that has been sealed for four and a half years lets a smell out even when you shut the lid again.
So here is everything I have got about the fourth of November, 2017, and the week after it, laid out honestly, with the holes marked.

What I have. Not the kitchen. I want to be scrupulous, because you'll get the kitchen later and I don't want any credit for having had it early. In April of 2022, sitting on that floor, what I had of that night was: an evening, an argument, a door. A grey area with a shape to it and nothing inside it. The overhead light with the moths in it, the burnt pan, the storm door shut behind the open back door, the two bags — none of that came back to me until the fourteenth of January, 2023, on wet concrete three hundred feet under the flats. What I have always had is the knock.

Ten past one in the morning, complete, every frame, and I have often wished I could trade some of it for something else. Two of them. A trooper and a Chicago officer, because of where the road is and where the house is. The trooper was a woman about thirty with her hat off and held against her chest, which they do, which is a thing they are taught, and which I did not know was a thing they are taught until 2019, when somebody told me, and it ruined something.
She said, "Are you Sean Vardy," and I said yes, and she said, "Is your wife Nuala Vardy," and I said yes. And then here's the part I would give a hand for.
She said: "Do you know where your wife was travelling tonight, sir?" And I said something. And I do not have what I said.

That's a hole. That's the second hole, and it sits four feet from the first one. Between a doorway with two bags in it and a trooper on my step there are three and a half hours, and out of the whole of that I have got a knock, a hat held against a chest, and a question I cannot hear my own answer to.

What was I doing at ten past one in the morning? Was I asleep? Was I in the chair? Had I been calling her? The phone was in the effects bag with a cracked screen, and I never looked at the log, and by the time it occurred to me to look, the carrier had cycled it, and that is a fact I sit with more often than most of the ones in this book.
What I did that week. I was, everybody agrees, magnificent.

I want to put it that way because it's the only word that fits and because it makes me want to be sick. Bernie has said it. Colleen has said it. My mother-in-law, who did not like me, held my face in both hands at the wake and said, "You have been a rock."

I did the funeral home. I chose a casket and I did not pause over the price list, I went straight down the middle column like a man ordering for a table. I dealt with Zaremba, who is a decent man with a strange handshake. I called eleven people on the fifth and told them in a clear voice and did not once make anybody comfort me. I wrote the notice. I found the dress. I stood at the door of Zaremba & Sons for two hours and forty minutes on the eighth of November and shook every hand that came through it and remembered every name. God, Sean was incredible. That's what people said in cars going home.
And I have since learned enough about myself to know what that actually was.

It was the parking. It was the same functioning administrative thing that worked out the short-stay charge while my son went cold against my shirt, running at full capacity for six days, doing logistics, because logistics was the only building in me with the lights on.

Nobody at a funeral can tell the difference between a man being strong and a man not being there. I've checked. It is exactly the same performance from the outside, there is no test for it, and the whole of American mourning is built on nobody knowing that. The ninth of November. Holy Cross. Rain, a canopy, a poor turnout of umbrellas.
And here's the thing about Holy Cross that I have never said to anybody, including the two people I have told the rest of this to. They are eleven rows apart.

Fionn's is one of the small flat ones and hers is upright, and if you stand at hers and look southwest you can see his, and I have not once in seven years walked from one to the other. I go to hers. I stand there. Then I go back to the truck the long way round the drive so I don't pass him.
And the storm door. That was in the drawer too, that April, and I did not go near it for a year.

One line in the report, taken down by a trooper at about two in the morning from an eighty-one-year-old woman who had been watching television with the sound up: neighbor reports hearing storm door twice.

I read it in April of 2022. I felt nothing at all and I put the paper back, and here's what my head did with it, in three seconds, no effort, the way the stomach handles food: She went out, she came back for something, she went out again. Women always come back for something.

I want that written down exactly as it arrived, because I want you to see how good it was. It isn't just an explanation. It has a little joke tucked inside it — an affectionate, marital joke, the kind of thing a man says at a wake and everybody laughs and nobody looks at anybody.
I built the joke, and the joke did the sealing. That's the trade in this house. That's what I have instead of a cutman.
And here is what I know now, which I did not know then, which nobody but me can know, and which I will never be able to check: There is no storm door on the front of that house.
There never has been. It's a solid door with a screen in the summer and no screen in the winter, and by the fourth of November there is no screen.
The storm door is at the back. The back, where the driveway is. The back, where the hook is.

So Mrs. Zabrocki, eighty-one, next door, with the television up, heard the back door of this house bang twice on the night my wife left it. And the trooper wrote one line. And Mrs. Zabrocki died in 2020.
And I read that sentence in 2022 and made a joke about women.
22. Turning It Off
May. Fight seven. A function room over a Polish social club in Archer Heights, gloved, which Gaz offered me as a soft one because he thought I looked like shit, which I did.
And this is the chapter where I did the thing on purpose, so let me not dress it up.

There is a move — it isn't a move, it's an absence of a move — where you simply stop bringing the hand back. The right hand lives at your cheekbone. That's its whole job. You throw it, it comes home. You throw it, it comes home. Thirty-four years of throw-and-home, ten thousand hours of it, until it isn't a decision, until it's the same order of reflex as blinking.

And you can turn it off. It takes real work. It's like deliberately not catching something thrown at your face — the body puts up an argument, and the argument is not in words, it's a rising heat in the chest and a total unwillingness of the arm — and you have to override it, consciously, punch by punch, for about ninety seconds, and then it gives up and stays down.
I turned it off in the third minute against a twenty-seven-year-old bricklayer named Milo Ganz.

He didn't understand at first. That's the thing nobody tells you about a man who won't defend himself: it frightens the other guy. Milo threw a straight right at four minutes and it went through where my hand should have been and landed flush on the cheek, and I saw his face afterward, and his face said, what.
I nodded at him. I actually nodded at him, like a man saying go on.

He hit me nineteen times in the next six minutes and I am not going to pretend I know how many of those I let happen and how many I couldn't have stopped, and that ambiguity is a mercy I have chosen to keep.

Here's the damage. The right cheekbone went. Not the arch this time — the body of it, the big flat shelf of bone under the eye that gives a face its shape — and it went in with a sensation exactly like a stone hitting a windshield, a sharp bright tock that I heard through the bone of my own head rather than through my ear. When that bone depresses, the face changes shape. The cheek flattens. Afterward, in the mirror, one side of my head looked like a chair somebody had sat on wrong.
And there's a nerve under there, the same one from Beecher, so the whole quadrant went numb again, and this time it stayed numb, and it is numb now, and it will be numb in the ground.

And the eye on that side stopped being level with the other one. About three millimeters low. Nobody notices unless I take my glasses off. Denny noticed in the corner and said nothing and I saw him not say it.

At minute twelve Milo Ganz put me down with a left hook and the ref, a guy named Stack, waved it off at four. VISIT FIVE. On the stool, according to Denny. Two and a half minutes. The kitchen. Four o'clock. The cardigan.
She said: "Sean, did you move my keys? They're not on the hook."

That's all. She didn't turn around. I got the back of her, and her voice, and about three seconds of the tongue in the cheek at the very end, in profile, and then it was gone. Two and a half minutes for a cheekbone.

And on the drive home I did the thing I always did, which was the math, and the math said the exchange rate had moved again, and I said out loud in the truck, to nobody, with a face that had begun collapsing on one side: "Fine. It's a seller's market." And then I laughed for about two miles.

I want that on the record too, alongside everything else. I was having, in some horrible way, the time of my life. Nobody ever writes that part down either. They write the misery. There's misery, sure, there's a whole warehouse of it. But there was also a man of forty-five, driving north on Cicero at midnight with a broken face and eight hundred dollars, who had a purpose for the first time since 2015, who woke up in the morning with something to do, who had stopped watching television with the sound down.

Grief is boring. That's the thing they leave out of the pamphlet. It is unbelievably, crushingly, hour-by-hour boring, four years of it, and what I had found was not happiness, it was not even relief. It was interest. I was interested again. You'll do a hell of a lot to stay interested. Ask anybody.
23. Ostrowski
Roofing, since it has paid for most of my life and nobody in this account has done a day's work yet.

Waldemar Ostrowski has a crew of six and a yard in Burnham and he has had me on and off since 2011. The arrangement is that he calls and I go and he pays cash on Friday, and in eleven years neither of us has mentioned my face.

Season's April to November. Tear-off and re-lay, mostly. Two-flats and bungalows on the East Side and out over the Indiana line, and now and then a flat roof on a commercial building, which is hot material and a different job entirely.
Here's what a tear-off is, since everybody has one over their head and nobody has watched it done.

You go up at seven with a roofing spade — a flat blade with teeth cut into it and a fulcrum welded underneath — and you drive it under the shingles and lever, and they come up in a sheet with the nails still in them, and you push that sheet down the pitch and off the edge into a dumpster twelve feet below. You do that from the ridge down, all day, bent at the waist, in whatever the weather is, and by three in the afternoon you have moved about four thousand pounds of material with your arms.

Then you sweep the deck and check for rot and lay felt and start nailing, and a good man does a bundle every twelve minutes with a coil gun, and the gun runs on a hose, and the hose is a trip hazard, and every man on that roof has a story about the hose.
In June of 2022 I did nine days on a two-flat on Green Bay Avenue with three cracked ribs from a scrap yard in Riverdale.

You cannot do it. That's the honest answer. Every movement on a roof is a torso movement — the lever, the sweep, the reach, the getting up off one knee — and a cracked rib draws a red line through the entire trunk. So what you do instead is find the ways to cheat. You work off both knees instead of bending. You breathe out before every lever. You take the gun and stay on the shallow sections and let the young ones have the pitch. And by the fourth day the whole crew has quietly redistributed the work around you and not one person has said a word about it, which is worse than if somebody had.
Ostrowski came up the ladder on the fifth day. Fifty-eight years old, went up it like a squirrel.

He watched me for a while and then he said, in the accent, which after thirty years in this country is entirely intact: "Sean. Is it the ribs or the head?" "Ribs." "Which." "Three and four." He nodded. He'd had four of them off a scaffold in 1996. Then he said: "You know I had a brother." "I didn't."

"Older." He said the name, and it is an extremely common name where he comes from, and it means nothing, and I still had to sit down on a roof in 2023 when I worked out that I had been fighting a boy with the same one. "He is in the ground in Gdansk since 1989. Twenty-six years old. He did it slowly, over about four years, with vodka, and everybody watched him do it, and everybody said — ach, it's the times. It's the shipyard. It's the country." He looked out over the roofs toward the lake.
"That's the only thing I will ever say to you about your face," he said. "So now I have said it."

And he went back down the ladder and kept me on the crew for the rest of the season and never raised it again. He paid me on Fridays. And in October, when I could not remember which house we were on and drove to Green Bay Avenue instead of Ewing, he moved me to ground work — sorting, loading, cutting — without any discussion at all, at the same money.
I found out in 2024 that it had not been the same money. He'd been topping it up out of his own pocket since August.
That's the part that gets me, looking back at all of it. Everybody knew.

That's what I keep running into. Denny knew by December of 2021. Ostrowski had the whole diagnosis by June of 2022, off a roof, in one sentence, with no medical training whatsoever. Gaz Tunney knew and put it in a spreadsheet. Colleen knew something and could not get it out of me on a Wednesday phone call. Aurel Duca knew — I saw it go across his face in September when he was standing over me and would not throw.
There was not one person in my life who was fooled by me. Not one, at any point, for a single week.

The only man on this earth who did not know what Sean Vardy was doing was Sean Vardy, and he had a beautiful, fast, extremely well-supported argument about it that he could produce in under four seconds, on any occasion, in any weather, at any hour of the day or night.
24. A Small Denomination
June. Fight eight. Truck bay, Torrence, bare. His name was Hollis Deed and he was fifty-one years old.
I'm going to sit in this one for a while, because it is the ugliest thing in this book that happened inside a fight, and none of the ugliness is physical.

Fifty-one. And he'd had a stroke in 2016 — the left side of his face didn't move properly, the corner of his mouth sat lower, and there was a slowness down that whole side that you could see in the way he took his shirt off.

I knew that before I said yes. Gaz told me on the phone. Gaz actually told me, unprompted, which for Gaz Tunney is practically an intervention: he's had a stroke, Sean, in 2016, I'm just saying so it's said. And I said, "Fine."

I want to be precise about what "fine" was doing in that sentence, because it was not indifference. Indifference would be better. What it was doing was arithmetic: a fifty-one-year-old with a bad left side cannot hurt me enough, therefore this is a poor purchase, therefore I will need to make up the difference some other way.

That's what I was thinking. Not this is a man who has had a stroke. I was thinking: this is a small denomination. Minutes one to four. He was better than he had any right to be for about four minutes.

That happens with old fighters. The first four minutes come out of the file — the feet, the shoulder feint, the way he stepped off to the right after throwing — all of it intact, all of it from 1994, running on something that doesn't need the damaged parts. Hollis Deed had a beautiful little step-back-and-counter that he must have thrown ten thousand times before I ever turned pro.
And then the four minutes ran out, the way they do, and there was nothing behind them. Minutes four to nine. I beat him.

There's no other word and I've looked. He caught me twice, both on the temple, both good, and I felt the second one in my back teeth — and then I put him down with a right hand at minute six and he went down slowly, in sections, the way a man goes down when the message reaches his legs late.
And he got up.

He got up at fourteen because there was no one counting who cared, and he came forward with his hands where his hands used to be, and I put him down again at minute eight. And he got up again. Now here's the part.

I was not angry with him. There was no blood between us at all. I stood on that concrete looking at a fifty-one-year-old man with a lopsided face getting off his knees for the second time in a truck bay for four hundred dollars, and what I felt — and I'm going to write it exactly, and then I'm going to have to live in the same sentence as it — what I felt was irritation.

He wasn't giving me what I came for. That was the entire content of my emotional life at that moment. This man was being hit insufficiently hard by me, which meant I was going to have to keep hitting him, which was taking time, and none of it was going to earn me a visit, and I could feel the whole evening going to waste.

There is a version of me from 2006 who would have gone to the referee. There's a version from 2014 who would have looked at his corner. There was no referee and he had no corner, so what was actually required was for the other man in that circle to be a person, and the other man in that circle was gone, and had been since December.
I put him down a third time at nine minutes with a left hook to the body that he did not see because it came from the dead side. And Gaz Tunney waved it off himself.

Gaz. Five foot six, quarter-zip, phone in each hand, a man who had never in his life stopped anything. He came in off the edge with his arms out saying "that's it, that's it, that's it," and he got between me and a man on the floor, and he looked at me.
I have thought about that look for a long time. It was not disgust. Gaz didn't have disgust in him; it wasn't in the product line.
It was the look of a man realising he has been selling something that has gone off.
VISIT SIX.
The kitchen. But the light was wrong.
Not the four o'clock gold. A flatter light, an overcast light, and the room was slightly the wrong size.
I want to stop on that, because it is the first genuinely frightening thing that happened in one of these and I sailed straight past it at the time.

Kitchens do not have sizes in memories. Nothing does. A remembered room has no dimensions — you never think and it was eleven feet across, you just have the room, all at once, from no particular position. Dimensions are a thing that gets supplied. Dimensions mean somebody has built the room, out of parts, and made decisions about it.

This one had dimensions and they were wrong. It was too long, and the ceiling was low, and I was standing somewhere I had never stood in that kitchen in my life. She said: "Sean, did you move the keys." Not my keys. The keys.
And the sentence didn't go up in the middle. It went along, and then it stopped, like something read off a card. Forty seconds, total.
And I got up off the floor of a truck bay having just beaten a stroke survivor half unconscious in front of sixty men, and drove home, and what I thought about the whole way was the ceiling height.
25. Six Minutes
July. Fight nine. The barn out past Beecher again — the same barn, the same pole construction, the same dirt.

In December it had been twenty-six degrees in there and you could see everybody's breath hanging in the rafters. In July it was ninety-four, and the dirt floor had gone to dust, and eighty men standing in a ring three deep had kicked that dust up into a fog that hung at head height under two work lamps and never settled all night. Everybody coughing. You could taste the floor before anything started.
His name was Ruell Sanchez and he was twenty-four years old.

Twenty-four. I want that to sit there on its own for a second the way it sat in me. I was a professional fighter before this man could read. Minutes one to four. He was quick and he was wild and he threw everything from too far away, and I was picking him off, and for about three minutes I was actually enjoying myself, which by July was rare. Minute four. And then he hit me.

I have no memory of the punch. I have Denny's account and I have a fifteen-second video somebody took on a phone that I watched once in 2023 and will not watch again. It was a right hand, thrown from the hip, with no technique in it whatsoever, and it landed on the jaw about an inch forward of the hinge. Minutes four to ten. Gone.

Not blurred. Not hazy. Gone. Six minutes with nothing in them at all. There is no film, there are no fragments, there is not even the sense of time having passed. Minute four runs directly into minute ten in me like a splice.
And Denny told me afterward — sitting in the Buick with the doors open and the dome light on, at half past two in the morning — that in those six minutes I fought quite well.
That is the single most disturbing sentence anybody has ever said to me and I have had a doctor tell me I overwrote my dead wife.

Because think about what it means. Somebody kept my guard up for six minutes. Somebody moved my feet, and slipped a right hand, and stepped off to the left twice, and threw a jab that Denny says was "the best one you threw all night." Somebody in there ran an entire fight — competently, adaptively, against a live opponent — and it was not me.

I was not present. There's nobody home in those six minutes. And yet the machine went on operating at a professional standard in a barn in Will County, and the crowd could not tell, and Sanchez could not tell, and the only man in that building who knew that Sean Vardy had left the premises was Sean Vardy, four hours later, in a car, being told about it.

I have never found out who that is. I don't like knowing he's in there. And I have thought more than once, at three in the morning, that if the lights are ever going to go out on me for good, that fellow is presumably going to be the last one standing at the switch, running the place with nobody in it — and that is my honest picture of what's coming, and it is not a metaphor, it's just a description with a date missing. Minute thirteen. The jaw.

Left side, at the angle, which is the corner where the jawbone turns up toward the ear. It's the most common place a jaw goes, because it is the thinnest part of a long lever and the lever is eleven inches long.

You know instantly, and not from pain. You know because your bite is wrong. The teeth on that side come together before the teeth on the other side, by a couple of millimetres, and your whole mouth is now a door that doesn't fit its frame. You close it and something inside meets something else too early and there's a small dead click, and you keep closing it, over and over, the way you keep touching a chipped tooth.

I finished it. Fifteen more minutes, on a broken jaw, in ninety-four degrees, in a fog of dust that I was breathing through a mouth I could not properly shut. Sanchez put me down at twenty-eight minutes and I got up and he put me down at minute thirty and they called it for him.
VISIT SEVEN.

The kitchen. Flat light. Wrong dimensions. Too long, ceiling too low. "Sean, did you move the keys." Pause. "Sean, did you move the keys." Pause. "They're not on the hook. They're not on the hook." Twenty seconds. Maybe less.
And I came back on the dirt of a barn in Will County with dust in my open mouth and a jaw that didn't fit, and I was crying.
Which I had not done for my son, and had not done at my wife's funeral, and had not done once in four and a half years.
I want to be honest about why, because it was not grief and it would be a great comfort to me if it had been.
It was the way you cry when the tank runs dry on a highway a long way from anywhere. It was supply.
Denny got down on the dirt next to me — sixty-six years old, both knees, in the dust, in ninety-four degrees — and put his hand on the back of my neck and said, "All right. All right, kid."
Twenty-six degrees in that barn in December and ninety-four in July, and Denny Fewster in both of them, holding a bucket, calling me kid.
26. Maintenance

Since we're being thorough, here's the machine shop. This is what a man of forty-five does to a body between fights to keep it able to take the next one, and there is not one thing in this chapter a doctor would sign. Sleep. Sitting up, on the couch, on the left side if the ribs are right and the right if they're left, with a cushion under whichever arm the hand is on. Four to five hours a night in the first week after a fight, because you keep waking when you roll. Eleven to fourteen hours a night from about day nine, because the head demands it and there is no arguing with the head. I lost most of 2022 asleep and could not tell you one dream out of it. Ice. Twenty on, twenty off, first forty-eight hours, and after that it does nothing and everybody does it anyway because it feels like doing something. Bag of peas. The same bag of peas, December 2021 to January 2023, refrozen four hundred times, gone grey and welded into a single lump — and if you'd told me at any point in those thirteen months that the peas were the saddest object in the house I'd have laughed at you, and I'd have been wrong. Pain. Here's the honest ledger, and it's the one part of this book where I'm going to be careful, because I know what happens when a man puts numbers in print.

Not opiates. I want that stated, and not out of virtue. I looked at that door twice and both times it shut for a stupid and entirely practical reason, which is that a man with a habit gets sloppy — and a sloppy man doesn't get up at nine, doesn't finish, and stops getting booked. And I needed to keep getting booked.
Sit with that a second. My addiction had a commercial interest in me staying clean. That is not sobriety. That's a rival firm.

So: the over-the-counter stuff, in the wrong amounts, for thirteen months. The anti-inflammatory sort in the morning, which chews a stomach, so you eat first, and then it chews the stomach anyway, and by September of 2022 I was passing something that looked like coffee grounds and I looked it up on a phone at two in the morning and then put the phone face down.

And the other kind at night, the paracetamol kind, which does nothing for a bone and takes the edge off a head, and which quietly takes a liver apart at doses that don't feel dramatic at all, because they are printed on the side of an ordinary box in a font nobody has ever read. Drink. Four to six a night in the first week after, then off it entirely, because alcohol thins blood and a thin man cuts worse and bleeds longer. I was managing a face, not a mood. Food. Eggs.

That's not a bit. From about April of 2022 I ate eggs, toast, and whatever the crew had at lunch, and that was the diet, because a shop is a sequence and a recipe is a sequence and I could not hold one. You'd find me in an aisle at eight at night with a basket and no idea what was supposed to go in it. Eggs you can do without a plan. The neck. The one genuinely intelligent thing I did in thirteen months, and I did it for the wrong reason.

A strong neck holds the head steadier. A steadier head means the brain travels less inside the skull when you're hit, and less travel means less damage. That is real, it is the single best thing a fighter can do for his own long-term head, and almost nobody does it because it isn't glamorous and there's no bag for it.
So I trained my neck. Every day, in a garage that leans, with a strap and a plate. Forty-five years old, in January, doing neck work in the cold. In order to take more.

There it is. I want that sitting alongside everything else in this chapter. I wrecked my stomach and my liver on drugstore pills, slept upright for a year, and ate nothing but eggs — and the one correct, evidence-based, doctor-approved thing I did with my body across the whole of it, I did so I could absorb more punishment before losing consciousness.
That's addiction, if anybody wants a definition and doesn't want to hear about chemicals.

It is not that you stop taking care of yourself. It's that the caretaking gets recruited. Everything in you that still works — every good habit, every scrap of discipline, every piece of hard-won professional knowledge — none of it gets destroyed. It gets hired. The whole plant is retooled and goes on running beautifully, at capacity, with excellent quality control, producing the one product that is killing you.
I have never in my life been fitter, sharper about my own body, or more disciplined than I was in the autumn of 2022. I was thirteen weeks from a bleed on the brain.
27. Just a Man Who Watched
The jaw was wired for five weeks and that is its own chapter of hell, which I'll spare you except for three details, because you're going to need to know how a mouth works later.

One: they don't wire it shut anymore, mostly, they plate it — they put a titanium strip along the break and screw it in through an incision inside your mouth so there's no scar on the outside, and it's a marvel, and I don't have any money, so they wired mine. Arch bars on the top and bottom teeth and steel loops between them, and you carry a pair of wire cutters in your pocket at all times in case you throw up, because if you throw up you drown.

Two: five weeks of liquid through a straw and I lost nineteen pounds, which at my weight is a lot of the wrong kind, and the wrong kind is muscle around the neck, and neck is the only thing on a fighter's body that has anything to do with protecting his head. A strong neck holds the skull steady and the brain doesn't slosh as far. So I came out of that five weeks lighter, weaker in the exact place that mattered, and more fragile than I had been at any point in my life.
Three: I did the math on that too. I did the math and the math said good. Denny came over on the twenty-second of August.

He didn't come in. That's how I knew. Denny Fewster had walked into my kitchen without knocking since 2013 and on the twenty-second of August 2022 he stood on the step with his hands in the pockets of a windbreaker and would not come past the door. "Gaz says you're on for September," he said. "Mm." "Say it out loud." "I'm on for September." "Bare?" "Bare." "Your jaw came out of a wire twelve days ago."
I said the line I'd prepared. I'd had it ready for a week, which should tell you everything.
"It's healed. It's plated with bone now, Denny, it's stronger than it was —"

"Don't." He said it quietly and it stopped me dead. "Don't do the medical thing. You've been doing the medical thing at me since Beecher. You know more about a face than any man I ever met and you've been using it like a lawyer."
We stood there. There was a bird going in the hedge that hasn't been cut since 2017. "I'm not doing it anymore," he said. "Doing what." "The corner. The bucket. The cuts. I'm not doing it."

I did the worst thing I have ever done to another human being and I did it in about four seconds and without any planning at all, which is how you know it came from somewhere real. I said: "Then you're just a guy who watched."
Denny didn't move. It was a hot morning and the light was flat.
"For thirty-four years," he said, "that's exactly what I was."

And then, because he is a better man than me and always was: "Your brows are gone, Sean. There's no skin left in either one, it's all scar, it's tissue paper over a doorframe. Your right cheek's dropped. And you've got a thing in your left eye, a tremor, it comes and goes, I've been watching it since June and I'm telling you now because I'm not going to be there to watch it anymore." He took a breath. "Somebody's got to do the cuts. Get whoever. Don't let it be a friend of Gaz's, they'll superglue you, and superglue in a brow means the next one opens twice as wide."
He turned around and went down the two steps and stopped on the path.
"Marge used to talk to me," he said, without turning. "After. In the house. Two, three years. I'd hear her upstairs going through the closet. Hangers going along the rail."

I didn't say anything. I stood in the doorway of my house and I did not say anything, because if I opened my mouth I was going to ask him how did you get her to keep doing it, and some very small piece of me that was still working knew that was the last sentence I could ever say to Denny Fewster.
"You could have told me," he said. "I'd have understood it better than anybody alive."
And he got in the Buick and drove up Baltimore Avenue, and that was the last conversation we had for seven months, and it is the one I'd take back over all the others.
PART THREE: THE BELL
28. The Second City
There is a second city underneath this one and almost nobody who lives up here has ever seen a foot of it.

Not the subway. Not the freight tunnels under the Loop that everybody knows about because they flooded in ninety-two. Deeper. There are bores down in the bedrock under this whole region, cut through solid dolomite three hundred feet down, thirty feet across, miles and miles of them, dug to swallow what comes off the streets when it rains so the river doesn't turn around and put itself in people's basements. They've been digging them since the seventies. Some parts got finished and some parts got started and stopped when the money moved, and there are shafts and side chambers and access galleries down there that were poured for a purpose and then left, and there is no map of all of it in any one man's hands.

I never learned what the room was for. I asked once, early, and a guy said "it's a valve house" and another guy said "it was never a valve house," and after that I stopped asking, because it did not matter and because the not knowing was, in a way I couldn't have defended, part of it. Here's how you get there.

You park in a lot off a service road in the industrial flats where nobody has any reason to be at ten at night and you walk about four hundred yards along a fence with the weeds up past your knees. There's a gate with a chain on it that has been cut and rejoined with a padlock that is not the county's padlock. Behind the gate is a concrete apron and a steel headhouse the size of a two-car garage with no windows and a door that has been unbolted and rebolted so many times that the bolt holes are all wallowed out.
Inside the headhouse the sound changes immediately. Everything gets close and slightly wet-sounding.

There's a cage. An open steel basket about six feet square hung on a cable, with a bar across the front, and it is run off a hoist that somebody's cousin maintains and I am not going to tell you how I feel about that. Six men at a time. You put your hands on the bar because there is nothing else, and a man up top pulls a lever, and you go down. It takes about ninety seconds.
The first thirty you can still see the mouth of the shaft above you, a square of orange city sky getting smaller like something being closed.

Then it goes. And then you are in a shaft with rock walls two feet from your face going up past you in the beam of somebody's flashlight, wet rock, streaming, and there's a smell that comes up to meet you that is the smell of the actual planet — cold stone and standing water and iron — and under it, faintly, sewage, not fresh, old, a sort of sweet gray ghost of it that gets into your clothes and comes home with you and is still in the truck in the morning.
Your ears go. Everybody's do. Men swallow and yawn on the way down like a plane coming in.

And the temperature drops and then it stops dropping and holds — it's about fifty-four degrees down there in December and about fifty-four in July, because three hundred feet of rock does not care what month it is — and that steadiness is the first genuinely unnatural thing about the place. Everything alive up here is seasonal. Down there it is one temperature forever.
Then the cage stops with a bang and you get out into the gallery.

Sodium lamps on stands, four of them, run off a generator two hundred feet up the drift so the noise of it is a low constant grinding underneath everything, felt more than heard, like being inside a stomach. Sodium light is orange and it does something specific to human skin: it takes the red out. Every man down there looks slightly like a photograph of himself. Blood looks black. That's not a figure of speech. Blood on the concrete under sodium light is black, and it stays wet-looking for hours because nothing evaporates down there, and by the end of a night the floor has these black continents on it that the next crowd stands in.

The room itself is a chamber maybe sixty by thirty with a curved ceiling and walls of poured concrete gone the color of an old tooth, and every surface has water on it. Not dripping — sheeting. It comes through the joints in a slow permanent seep and runs down the walls in sheets that shine, and it collects along the base and runs off somewhere and you never see where. The whole room is quietly, continuously raining down its own sides.
The air is thick and it tastes like a coin. You breathe it for six hours and you cough for two days.

There's no ring. There's a circle of men, a hundred and forty of them by the end, standing in the wet with their breath in the orange light, and they don't shout the way they shout in a truck bay because you can't — the sound comes back at you off a curved ceiling, and a hundred and forty men making noise in a concrete tube is unbearable, physically, so the crowd down there stays low, and what you get instead is this constant close murmur, right up against you, like men talking in the next room in a hospital at four in the morning. And there's the bell.

It's a locomotive bell. Bronze, about nine inches, on a bracket welded to a piece of angle iron driven into a wall anchor. Somebody found it somewhere. It has a rope on it. There is one bell to start. There is one bell at the end. And the end is when a man does not get up.

That's the whole ruleset. There are no rounds. There is no minute. There is no stool, no count, no ref pulling you off, no doctor at the apron, no towel, because there is no corner to throw it from. Two men go into a circle of a hundred and forty in a wet concrete room three hundred feet under Illinois, and it goes on, continuously, without pause, until one of them is on the floor and stays there. I want you to sit with that for a second, because I did.

Everything I had done up to that point had an architecture to it. Rounds are mercy. A count of twenty is mercy. A referee is mercy. Even in a barn in Beecher there was a structure that periodically stopped the damage and asked you, in effect, do you want to keep doing this, and you had to answer yes, out loud, with your body, every single time. Down there nobody asks you anything.

The first time I stood in that room, in September, with the murmur going round the walls and the water sheeting and the generator grinding away up the drift and my breath orange in front of my face, I felt something I have to describe accurately, and the accurate description is embarrassing. I felt welcomed.

Because I had been trying for ten months to find a place with no mercy in it, and I had been buying it in ugly little increments off Gaz Tunney like a man scoring pills, and here was a room, purpose-built, three hundred feet below the city where I was born, where the whole concept had simply been left out of the design.
The ceiling down there is the entire weight of Chicago. Everything: the streets, the yards, the schools, the churches with the copper roofs,
Holy Cross Cemetery where my son is, Baltimore Avenue, the hedge, the house with four rooms in use.
All of it directly above your head, all of it off, all of it somebody else's problem, for as long as this takes. I have never been anywhere so quiet in my life.
29. The Hundred and Forty

Somebody should account for the men in that room, because I was one of them for four months before I was ever in the middle of it, and because the whole thing only works if a hundred and forty people agree to stand in a wet concrete tube under the city and watch.
Nobody goes down a shaft on a ladder and a cable at eleven at night in November by accident.

Here's the arithmetic of the room, because it is all arithmetic down there and I was the only man who ever said so out loud. Twenty dollars at the top. A folding table in the headhouse and a man with a coffee can. A hundred and forty men is twenty-eight hundred dollars, which pays the fighters, the generator, the diesel, the hoist man, and Gaz's cut, and leaves enough over that somebody down there was doing well and I never found out who. The betting. That's the real economy and it goes on in a low murmur off the walls. Not a bookmaker — men, in twos and threes, in cash, with a third man holding it, and I want to be clear that on the fourteenth of January, 2023, when I fought Marek Sowinski, money changed hands in that room on the question of whether I would get up, and the men holding the middle of those bets were standing eleven feet from me while I did it. Who they are. Not gangsters. I want that stated because it's the assumption and it's wrong and the truth is much worse.

Tunnel guys and their brothers-in-law. Operating engineers. Two firefighters I recognised from a card in Cicero. A man who did tile with Duca. Guys off the crews at the refinery, guys from the barges, guys who work nights at the intermodal yard in Harvey and finish at ten and have nowhere to put the rest of themselves. Men in Carhartt with reading glasses pushed up on their heads. Men in their sixties. A guy with an oxygen concentrator he'd left in his truck because he wasn't carrying it down a ladder.
I have never in my life been in a room with a lower proportion of people I would call dangerous. That's the thing. That's the thing that took me months to work out.
They are not there for violence. They can get violence anywhere in this city for free.
What they're there for. I worked it out in October, standing at the back with a face like a road accident, watching two men I didn't know go for nineteen minutes.
They're there because there is no arrangement left, anywhere in the ordinary world above that ceiling, in which a man is permitted to find out what he actually is.

Everything up there is insured. Everything is licensed and padded and stopped early by a man in a shirt, and I'm not against any of that — I'd have had the retina at thirty-three either way. But there is a thing in men, and I've had it since 1988, which is a question, and the question is: how much? How much of it can I take before I'm not me anymore, and where exactly is that line, and what's on the other side of it?
Nearly every man will go his whole life without an answer. That's not a tragedy, it's just an unpaid bill, and most of them carry it fine.
But it's a bill, and a hundred and forty of them went down a hole in the ground on a Saturday night to watch somebody else settle it in cash.

That's what they murmured for. Not for the blood — you can tell, the blood quiets them. What lifts that room is a man getting up. Every time. Second knockdown, third, fifth, eleventh, and the noise comes off that curved ceiling and it is not a cheer and it is not bloodlust. It's relief.

Because if he can, then maybe you could. That's it. That's the whole transaction, a hundred and forty times over, twenty dollars each. And the other thing. There were men down there buying exactly what I was buying and we all knew it and not one of us ever said a word.

Duca had something. Threadgill had that scar on his throat from a night nobody ever asked about. Curtis Wardell was forty-five years old and came down a ladder in December for twelve hundred dollars, and nobody does that for twelve hundred dollars. Hollis Deed had had a stroke and he still got up twice off a floor in a truck bay, and I hated him for it at the time, and I understand now that what I was looking at was a man with the same disease, at a different stage, being served by the same supplier.
There is a whole culture down there and its single organising rule is that you never ask a man why he's here.

I used to think that was hardness. It isn't. It's the last piece of decency any of us had left — because every man in that room understood, without being told, that the why was the only thing anybody had that could still be taken off him. And this. In four months I never once saw a woman in that room.

I don't have a clever thing to say about it. I just noticed it around November and I have thought about it since, and the nearest I've got is that whatever the hundred and forty of us thought we were doing down there, it required, absolutely and without exception, that nobody was watching who might have said what are you doing.
Three hundred feet of rock over your head does the same job as a locked bathroom door. That's all the tunnel ever was. It's just that there's more of it.
30. She Laughed
September. Fight ten. The first one down the shaft.

His name was Aurel Duca and he was thirty-three and he had come to this country at nineteen and he did tile work, and he weighed two hundred and twenty pounds, and I weighed a hundred and eighty-eight after the wire.

The man who did my cuts was called Vic. That's the whole of what I know about Vic. He had a fishing tackle box and a headlamp and hands like a plumber's, and he was competent in the way of a man who has done a thing without ever being taught it. The bell went.

Minute one to minute four, I boxed him. Genuinely. He was slow and he was square, feet in a line like a man reading a plaque, and I put the jab in his face maybe thirty times and moved off to his left and made him turn, and turning tires a big man faster than punching does. I split his lip in the third minute against his own teeth and I saw the black run down onto his chin under the sodium and I thought, I can win this.

That's the thing that catches you every time. Somewhere in the fourth minute of every one of these, the old animal wakes up and says, actually, let's win. Thirty-four years of training does not know it has been repurposed. Thirty-four years of training thinks we're still trying to get on television. Minute six he hit me on the top of the head.

I'd ducked, badly, and he was coming down with a right, and it landed on the crown, which is the hardest bone you have and the last place you want anything to land, because the neck is not built to take force straight down the column. Two things happened at once. His third and fourth knuckles broke — I heard it, and afterward his hand looked like a bag of marbles — and something in my neck went, some sheet of muscle behind the ear, and for the rest of the fight I could not turn my head to the left, so half the room became a place where things came from.
Minute nine to minute nineteen is the worst ten minutes of physical experience I have ever had and I include the jaw. He got me against the wall.

That's the specific thing about that room, and if you take one detail from this chapter take that one. There are no ropes, so there is nothing to lean on and nothing to bounce off, but there is a wall, poured concrete, running with water, and when a two-hundred-and-twenty-pound tile setter walks you back into it there is nowhere else in the world to be. Your shoulder blades are on wet concrete. Your heels have nothing behind them. The crowd is off to the sides, close enough to touch, murmuring. And he hit me for ten minutes.

Not continuously. Nobody can. He'd hit me eight or nine times and then he'd put his head on my chest and breathe, and I'd stand there holding a man up with my back against a wall three hundred feet underground, both of us wheezing like old dogs, and then he'd push off and start again, and we did that — I counted afterward, from what Vic told me and what I have — nine or ten times. The damage, in order.

Right brow, opened in the tenth minute, and it went to the bone straightaway because Denny was right, there was no skin left in it, just eight years of scar with no give in it at all, and scar doesn't split, scar parts, like a seam. Left brow, twelfth minute, same.

By minute thirteen I was blind in both eyes with blood, and Vic could not do anything about it, because there is no between. There's no round. There is nobody to wipe your face. You are simply a man in a room with blood in both eyes and no arrangement exists for fixing that, and so you fight blind, and you fight it by feel, forearm against his forearm, reading him off contact like a man in a dark house.

Fifteenth minute he broke the orbital rim over my left eye — that's the frame of the socket, the hard ring, and when the top of it goes there's a step in it afterward that you can feel with your thumb for the rest of your life, and I can feel it now, a little ledge, like a badly hung door.
Sixteenth minute, the nose again, fifth time, and this time it went flat rather than sideways.

Somewhere in the seventeenth I stopped being able to keep my hands up. Not decided. The arms went. There's a thing that happens where you tell the arm and the arm receives the message and does about forty percent of it, and there's no pain and no drama, they simply become somebody else's arms hanging on you.

And Aurel Duca, who was not a bad man, who was a tile setter with a broken hand three hundred feet underground, put me down at nineteen minutes with a right hand I did not see, and I went down on the wet concrete on my face. And the bell went.
VISIT EIGHT.

I have to tell you about this one properly. I owe it that. Because everything before it was a rehearsal and everything after it was a demolition, and this — this was the thing itself, the best four minutes of my adult life, and I am not going to be shy about it just because of what it turned out to be.
It was a Saturday. I knew it was a Saturday the way you know things in there, without being told.

The light in the kitchen was the four o'clock gold coming in over the sink, and there was dust turning over in it, and the radiator was ticking, and outside somebody two houses down was running a leaf blower, and there was a smell of the coffee that had been in the pot too long.

She was at the counter in the blue cardigan with her hair up in the elastic, and she was cutting the ends off flowers. That's what she was doing with her hands. She was cutting the ends off a bunch of supermarket flowers on the diagonal and dropping them in a jar, and I had not remembered that in four and a half years and there it was, the small green mess of the ends on the counter, the way she held the scissors like a knife.

And she turned around and she looked at me, and she was thirty-eight, she had the little vertical line she got between her eyebrows, and she said: "Sean, did you move my keys?" And I said, "They're in your bag."
And she said, "They're not in my bag, I looked in my bag, don't do the thing where you say the bag." And she laughed.

That's what I got. That's what came back that night, and had never come back before: she laughed. She put her head back about an inch and laughed at me in a kitchen in Hegewisch with green stems in her hand.
And I could smell her hair, and the coffee, and the cut stems.

And I said, "I love you," out loud, three hundred feet under Illinois, on a wet concrete floor with my face open in four places, and a hundred and forty men in the orange dark listening. She said: "I know. Help me find my keys." Four minutes and forty seconds. That was the last time she was ever real.
31. Going Up
Getting a broken man up out of that place is its own event and nobody thinks about it beforehand, including the men who run it.

You cannot carry somebody in the cage. There isn't room to lie down and there isn't a stretcher and there is no arrangement whatsoever, because the whole enterprise is predicated on nothing going seriously wrong, which is a thing that men in that room believed with the fervor of the religious right up until it did.

So two of them stood me up and put my arms over their shoulders and walked me the two hundred feet up the drift, and I was awake for that, in the sense that my eyes were open, and here is what that walk was:

Orange lamps behind me getting further away. A rock ceiling four feet over my head, wet, with a bolt pattern in it. Water running along the base of the wall on the left. The generator getting louder as we got closer to it and then unbearable as we passed it and then falling away. Black footprints on the concrete — my own, going the other way, from earlier, when I'd walked in. A hundred and forty men standing back against the walls in the dark to let us through, not saying anything, most of them, and a few of them saying good man, good man, which is what they say, which means nothing, which I have said myself.
And the taste of the air. Wet coin, and old sewage, and now blood as well, because my mouth and nose were full of it and every breath came through it.
They put me in the cage and one of them held me up by the back of the belt. Ninety seconds.
Going up is worse than going down, and I want to try to explain why, because it's the only part of that whole night that has stayed with me as a kind of nightmare rather than as a fact.
Going down, you're going somewhere. There's a destination and the shaft is a corridor.

Going up, you are a broken thing being raised through three hundred feet of rock toward a hole. And you can see the hole the whole way. It starts as nothing, a fleck, and it grows, and it is orange, because the sky over this city is always orange, and it comes down to meet you very slowly, and there is nothing to do for ninety seconds but hang on a bar and watch the world reopen above you, and I remember thinking, with a clarity I have not had since: You have to go back up there. She isn't up there.
That was the first time it came at me in exactly that shape. Not I want to see her again. Not I miss her. She's down here and I have to go back up.
You could not have told me a more dangerous sentence if you'd spent a year drafting it.

They put me in the back of somebody's Tahoe and a guy named Kev drove me to my truck and asked me four times if I wanted the hospital, and each time I said no, and on the fourth he said "your face is not right, man, your face is not right," and I laughed, and he stopped asking.
I sat in my own truck in a lot off a service road at five past two in the morning with the mirror pulled down and the dome light on and I looked at it.

Both brows open to the bone, gaping — not bleeding much anymore, just open, and you could see the pale in the bottom of the right one, which is the bone of the brow ridge, which I had never seen before, which does not look like anything, which looks like the inside of a shell.
Left orbital rim stepped. You could see it in the mirror as a change in the outline of my own face, like a fence with a post kicked out.
Nose flat and lying about fifteen degrees to the left of where God put it, and both eyes closing fast, the left already down to a slot.
Lips split top and bottom. Two teeth loose on the lower left, which I could rock with my tongue, and which I later lost.

And the swelling had already gone so far that there was no shape left to my face at all — no cheek, no jaw, no eye sockets, just a smooth risen mass with holes in it, the way a face looks in the last stage before it stops looking like a face, and I want to say plainly that if you had put a photograph of that in front of anybody who loved me they would have made a sound. And I sat there and looked at it and here's what I thought. I thought: she laughed.

I put the mirror up and I drove myself home to Baltimore Avenue through empty streets with one eye and a face like a dropped cake, and I was — I'm going to say it, because if I start lying here then all the rest of it is worthless — I was happy.

It's four in the morning in September and a man is driving north with his face destroyed, and he's happy, and the reason he's happy is that he has just spent four and three-quarter minutes in a kitchen with his wife, who laughed at him about her keys, and who has been in the ground at Holy Cross since the ninth of November 2017.
That's the middle of the story. Everything from here is the bill.
32. The Six Days

Six days between a wet floor three hundred feet under the flats and a chair in an office at Christ, and I spent them alone in a house in Hegewisch doing my own medicine, and somebody should write down once what that actually is. Night one, four in the morning. Home. Truck in the drive. I did not make it past the kitchen.

You cannot lie down. That's the first thing nobody tells you. A face in that condition is a pressure system, and horizontal is the worst thing you can do to it, so you sit — upright, on a kitchen chair, forearms on the table, head forward — because forward keeps the blood running out of the nose instead of down the back of the throat, and blood down the throat at that volume makes you vomit, and vomiting with a face like that is an experience I would put up against anything that happened in a fight.
I sat at that table from four in the morning until about nine, awake, upright, thinking about nothing at all, with a dish towel that started out white. Night one, later. The brows.

Both open. The right one to the bone along close to two inches. And it is four in the morning on a Sunday, and we have already established what an emergency room asks, and how many times it asks it, and who comes and sits down afterward.

So: kitchen sink. Hot water. Dish soap on the skin around it and never in it. You irrigate — that's the whole of wound care, and every field manual on earth says the same thing, the solution to pollution is dilution — so you fill a plastic cup and pour it in there, over and over, twenty cups, thirty. And it hurts in a way that being punched does not hurt, because it is slow, and because you are doing it to yourself, and because you can stop any time you like.

Out of the right brow came grit. Actual grit, off a floor three hundred feet down. And a piece of something black about the size of a match head, which I got with tweezers, and after which I sat on the bathroom floor for a while.

Then butterfly strips — six on the right, four on the left — which held about nine hours and then didn't, because a brow moves, and because the skin around them was too wet with the weeping a big wound does for the first two days.
Day two. The worst of it. Day two always is; the swelling peaks somewhere between thirty-six and forty-eight hours and then starts back down.
I could not open either eye. Worse than usual on the left, because the rim underneath it was broken, so the architecture had shifted and the lid wasn't sitting on anything.

I held it open with two fingers to look in the mirror, and what was in the mirror was not a face with injuries on it. It was a smooth risen thing, purple-black across the whole left side, going green-yellow down at the jaw, with a nose lying flat and off to one side, two wet red lines where eyebrows had been, and a mouth that was not centred.
I said, out loud, alone, in a bathroom: "Well. There goes the modeling."
I made that same joke four months later in a hospital bed in front of my sister and she laughed and then went out into the corridor.
Nobody heard it the first time. That's the thing about a man on his own. All the material's wasted. Day two, evening. The nose again.

Fourth time. You already know what it is and what happens if it stays in there, so I won't do the lecture twice — the short version is that the bridge of a man's nose has a shelf life once the blood is behind it, and mine was on the clock.
Denny had done this for me four times. Bathroom of his two-flat, syringe, needle flamed with a lighter, a paper cup, twenty seconds. Denny had stood on my step in August in a windbreaker.

I did it myself, at half past nine at night, in the bathroom on Baltimore Avenue, with a diabetic's needle from a pharmacy on Torrence and a flashlight held in my teeth, in front of a mirror, on the inside of my own nose.

I got about half of it. The angle is impossible on yourself. You cannot see up your own nose and hold a light and work a syringe with a hand that's missing a knuckle, and I gave up at ten minutes with maybe half of it out, and that is why the bridge on that side has a soft place in it now that gives under a thumb. Days three to five. The head.
This is the stretch that frightened me, and I want to be accurate about what frightened me, because it wasn't the pain.

Day three, I got up to make eggs and found the pan already on the burner, cold, with butter in it, and no memory whatsoever of putting it there. I stood in my kitchen and worked out from the state of the butter that it had been sitting there about an hour.
Day four, I talked to somebody on the phone about a bill for eleven minutes, hung up, and could not recall one word of it — including whether I had agreed to anything.
Day five, around six in the evening, I was standing in the hall and I did not know which way the front room was.
Two seconds. Maybe three. My own house. Thirteen years in it. I stood in the hall and had to work it out from the light.

That's the one. Everything else in this account you can argue with me about — the fights are a choice, the visits are a mystery, the arithmetic is at least arithmetic. But standing in your own hallway in the dark at forty-five years of age, not knowing where the front room is, six days after paying four minutes and forty seconds for a woman who does not exist — that isn't a transaction anymore.

That's a man going out like a pilot light, in the same house his father did it in, in the same front room, thirty-odd years later. And the only difference between Emmett Vardy and me is that it was done to him by a steel company, and I paid a man in a quarter-zip twelve hundred dollars a night for the privilege. Day six. The right brow went yellow at the edges and started to smell faintly sweet, which is a smell you only ever need described to you once, and I got in the truck and drove to Christ. Not because I was frightened for my brain.
Because I was frightened of losing the eye. And a man with one eye can't get booked.
33. No File
So on the sixth day I drove to Christ, because a wound that goes yellow at the edges is not a wound anymore, it's a situation, and I have seen what happens to men who let a face infection run.

They cleaned and closed both brows — twenty-two stitches on the right, fourteen on the left, done by a resident who was maybe thirty-one and who did not say one single word to me the entire time and whose jaw was set so hard I could see the muscle going. They scanned my head for the orbital rim. And somewhere in that process a name went into a system, and four hours later, when I was sitting in a corridor waiting to be discharged with a paper cup of pills, Parvaneh Ashkani came around the corner with a folder under her arm and stopped dead.
She didn't say anything for a while. She just looked at my face. "Come with me," she said.

Her office had a window that looked out at a parking structure. There was a photograph on the desk of two grown daughters at somebody's graduation and a small brass thing on the shelf that I later learned was a bird. "How many," she said. "Doc —" "How many since February." "Six." She sat back. "You told me four, in February. Total." "That was also a lie."

"I know it was a lie, Mr. Vardy, I put a mark on the paper." She took the glasses out of her hair and set them down, and she did it very carefully, and I understood that she was managing herself. "I want to say something to you and I want to say it without the kindness on it, because I gave you the kindness in February and you took it out of here and you used it."
I didn't say anything, because she was right, and because I hadn't known she'd worked that out.
"You asked me about your friend," she said. "The one who sees his wife." "Yeah." "There is no friend."
"No." "How many times?"

And I told her. I sat in a chair in an office with a view of a parking structure and I told another human being for the first time, out loud, all of it, from a VFW hall in Cicero in December through a barn and a scrap yard and a truck bay and a room three hundred feet under the flats, and the count, and the exchange rate, and the arithmetic on Christmas Day, and how it had started at nine seconds and one punch and was now up to nineteen minutes and two brows and a rim.
It took about nine minutes to say. Four and a half years and it fits in nine minutes.
When I stopped she was quiet for a long time. Then she said: "Eight times." "Eight."

"All right." She got a piece of paper and turned it sideways. "I'm going to tell you something now and I need you to understand that this is not the part where the doctor tries to frighten you into behaving. I'm long past that with you. This is a piece of information about how your head works that you don't have, and once you have it, everything you've told me means something different than what you think it means. Are you listening." "I'm listening."
"When you remember something," she said, "what do you think is happening?" "I'm — looking it up."

"Right. That's what everybody thinks. There's a thing in there, on a shelf, and you go and get it and you look at it and you put it back." She drew a small box on the paper. "That's not what happens. There's nothing on a shelf. There's no file. The memory doesn't exist anywhere as a whole object.
