It's kept in pieces — the picture in one place, the sound in another, the smell somewhere else entirely, the feeling of it somewhere else again — and when you remember, you build it. From parts. Right then. Fresh, every time." "Okay."

"So what you experience as looking at a photograph is actually more like — a workshop. Every single time you recall your wife, you are assembling her, from components, in the conditions of that moment."
"Fine. So?"

"So," said Parvaneh Ashkani, "here's the part nobody's told you. When you're done, it doesn't go back the way it was. It goes back the way you just built it. The version that gets saved is the version you just made. That's not a flaw, it's the design — it's how a memory can update, how you learn that the dog that bit you is dead now and stop being afraid. Every recall is a rewrite. Every single one. There is no way to look at a memory without changing it. It's not a photograph. It's more like — a story a family tells at Christmas. It's still true. But it's not the same as it was in 1994, and nobody in that family did anything wrong."
I sat there. Outside, a car went up a level of the parking structure.

"You are recalling your wife," she said, "under the worst conditions a human brain can be placed in. Not tired. Not drunk. Not sad. You are calling her up in a concussed brain, in the minutes after severe rotational trauma, in a state where your language is falling apart, your ability to hold a sequence is gone, your emotional tone is flattened, and the very structures that build memories are being physically shaken. That's the workshop you've been using. Eight times."
"But she's complete in there. Doc, she's more complete in there than she is anywhere —"

"Yes," she said. "I'm sure. That's what a seizure-like event feels like — it feels realer than reality, it always has, that's been documented for ninety years. That's not evidence she's intact. That's evidence of what's happening electrically in the part of your brain that produces the feeling of this is real." She leaned forward. "Mr. Vardy. When you noticed she said a word she'd never say. When you noticed the light was wrong. When she started repeating herself. What did you think that was?" "The venue," I said. "The connection."

"There is no connection," she said. "There's no line and there's no person on the other end. There is one copy of Nuala in this universe and it is in your head, and every time you go in there under a hammer, you come back out and you save over her."
I want to describe what that felt like physically because that's the only part I can describe.

There's a thing in a fight where you get hit and you don't feel it and you know from the sound — from what it sounded like inside your own skull — that in about a second and a half you're going to be in trouble. And there's that second and a half. And in it you're completely fine.
I had that. In the chair. "How much," I said. "How much what?" "How much of it's gone."
And she said the thing that I have thought about every day since, and she said it gently, and she didn't look away, which I have never forgiven her for and which was the correct thing to do.

"I don't know," she said. "And here's what I want you to understand and it's the worst part, so brace up. You can't know either. You have no independent copy to check against. You can't hold the new one up next to the old one, because the old one is what got written over. Whatever's in there now will feel exactly as true as what was in there in 2017. That's what it feels like from the inside. It always feels like the original." "So I can't tell."

"You can't tell. Nobody can tell. That's true for all of us all the time, incidentally, we're all doing this — but the rest of us are doing it slowly, in ordinary conditions, over decades." She put the pen down. "You've done four decades of drift in ten months, with a hammer." I said: "I've been overwriting her." "Yes." "Eight times." "Yes." "And it's permanent."
"There's nothing to restore from," said Parvaneh Ashkani. "You're it. You were the only copy of her, Sean. That's what a widower is."
34. Level Four
I did not go home. I sat in the truck in the garage at Christ, on level four, next to the elevators, for two hours and ten minutes.
And I want to lay out exactly what a man does with that, because I think people imagine there's a collapse, and there wasn't one, there was something much more efficient and much worse.

First I argued. For about forty minutes I argued with a woman who wasn't there, and I argued well, because I've had thirty-four years of being the guy who explains injuries, and I know how to sound like I know.

She said memory is rebuilt from parts. Fine. But some things don't degrade — the phone number of the house I grew up in, that's forty years old, it's fine, I can say it right now. So the whole everything drifts business is overstated. Certain things are welded in. Nuala is welded in.

She said the visits feel realer than reality because of what's happening electrically. Fine. But that cuts both ways. If a damaged brain can make something feel real that isn't, then a damaged brain can also reach something that a normal one can't. She can't have it both ways. She wants to say the damage produces a false thing, and I'm saying the damage produces a door, and neither of us can look inside, so it's her word against mine.

She said there's no independent copy. Fine, Doc. Then how do you know it's been overwritten? By your own argument you can't check either. You've got no more access than I have. All you've got is a theory about what ought to have happened to the tissue, and I've got four minutes and forty seconds of a woman cutting the ends off flowers.
That was the best one. I got to that one at around the eighty-minute mark and I actually said "there you go" out loud in an empty truck.
Then I did the arithmetic anyway. Because that's the trouble with arguing well. You win, and the winning takes forty minutes, and then there's the rest of the two hours.

Ten fights. Eight visits — I had thought of it as eight visits and Ashkani had said eight times and it was the same number and it was not the same number at all, and once you've seen that, you can't unsee it.
Visit one: four minutes, warm, complete. She turned around. The keys. The tongue in the cheek.
Visit two: four minutes. Warm. Same. Visit three: three minutes. Same. Visit four: anyway.
Visit five: two and a half. She didn't turn around. I got the back of her.
Visit six: the light was wrong. The kitchen had dimensions. The keys, not my keys. Forty seconds.
Visit seven: she said it twice. Then she said the hook line twice. Twenty seconds.
Visit eight: four minutes forty. Complete. The best one. The flowers. The laugh. And there it was.

That's what I'd been holding onto since September, without ever putting it in a row — it got better again. The degradation wasn't a line going down. Six and seven were rubble and then eight was the best of the whole lot. So the whole overwrite theory falls apart, doesn't it, because you cannot overwrite something into being more complete.
I sat in level four with my hands on the wheel and I felt the relief come up through me like heat off a road.

And then, somewhere around the two-hour mark, a very quiet part of me — the same part that had said that wasn't right about the word anyway, that same flat unimpressed employee who has been in there my whole life and has never once been wrong and has never once been listened to — that part said: Or you built a better one.

Not recovered. Not reached. Built. With more material, in a longer session, under a heavier hammer, in the finest workshop I'd ever had access to: nineteen minutes against a wall three hundred feet underground.
Six and seven were what the truth looked like when it was falling apart.
Eight was what a forgery looked like when it finally came out right.
I sat with that for about ninety seconds and then I did the thing I want on my headstone.
I said, out loud, in a parked truck on level four of a hospital garage, to nobody, with twenty-two stitches in one brow and fourteen in the other:
"Then it works."
Because look at it. Look at it honestly, from where I was sitting.

If the visits were her, then every one I bought was a theft from the last copy of my wife, and I was a man robbing a grave with his own head, and I'd already done it eight times and couldn't give any of it back.

But if I was building her — if that's all it ever was, an assembly job in a damaged room — then nothing was being destroyed at all. There was nothing there to destroy. She'd been gone since 2017 and the thing in the kitchen was a construction, and constructions can be improved, and visit eight was the proof, and the workshop was three hundred feet under the industrial flats and it was open every second Saturday and Gaz Tunney would put me on the card if I texted him. Do you see it? Do you see what it does?

Both answers pointed down the shaft. There was no version of the truth, none, that put me on a road going anywhere else. I had reasoned my way, in a parking garage, with genuine rigor, from a doctor telling me I was destroying my wife's memory to a solid intellectual foundation for going back and doing it four more times.
I want to say something for anybody who's ever loved somebody like me, because I've been on both sides of this and the other side is worse.

We are not stupid. That's the thing you have to give up. You keep waiting for us to understand, because you think this is a shortage of information, and you keep bringing more information, better information, a doctor, a scan, a printout.
We understand. We understood before you did. We're smarter about it than you are, we've thought about it more hours than you have, and we will out-argue you in front of any jury you like.
The intelligence isn't the brake. The intelligence is the engine.
I turned the key and went down four levels of ramp and paid fourteen dollars and drove home.
35. Rostam and Sohrab
I went back twelve days later to get the stitches out, which is a five-minute job done by somebody who does it forty times a week, and she found me in the corridor on the way out.
She had a coffee and a lanyard and the look of a woman nine hours into something. "Your face is healing badly," she said. "My face has been healing badly since 1991."
"I mean the rim. The step's setting. It won't come out now." "I know."

We stood there. It was the corridor between the elevators and the walkway, with the vinyl floor and the light that makes everybody look like they've been up all night, which everybody has. "You're going back," she said. I didn't answer, which is an answer.
She looked at her coffee. And then Dr. Parvaneh Ashkani did a thing I did not expect, which was that she said, "Do you know the Shahnameh?" "The what?"

"No. Of course not." She rubbed her eye. "It's a book. It's the book, where I'm from, it's a thousand years old, it's kings and heroes, it's a hundred thousand lines of poetry and my grandmother knew about a third of it by heart and I know about nine stories badly." She checked her watch and then visibly decided not to care about her watch. "There's one everybody knows. I'm going to tell it to you wrong. My grandmother would take my ear off." "Go on."

"There's a hero. Rostam. He's the greatest man alive, everybody knows him, he's the one they send when nobody else can do it. And when he's young he passes through a place and there's a woman, and he doesn't stay, and he leaves her a token — an armband, an onyx thing — and he says, if it's a girl, put it in her hair, if it's a boy, put it on his arm. And he goes.
"And it's a boy. Sohrab. And he grows up enormous and fearless and he grows up hearing who his father is, and everything he does, he does to find him.

"Years later, there's a war. And a young champion comes out on the other side, and nobody can beat him, and so they send for Rostam. And the two of them come out to the ground in front of both armies and they don't know each other. The boy asks. That's the thing that kills you. The boy asks — twice, three times, he says are you Rostam, because he's heard, and something in him knows — and the old man says no. Out of caution. Out of tactics. He gives a false name." She turned the coffee cup around.

"They fight for two days. And on the second day Rostam gets him down and puts a knife in him. And the boy is lying there dying and he says: my father is Rostam, and when he hears of this he will come for you. And Rostam tears his armor open and there's the armband on his arm." Somebody went past us with a cart.

"And that's not even the worst part," she said. "The worst part is what comes next. Because there's a remedy. There's a medicine in the king's treasury, and it works, everybody knows it works, and it would save the boy. And Rostam sends for it. And the king — who has his own reasons, who's frightened of Rostam, who is being small — the king delays. He doesn't refuse. He delays.
"And the medicine arrives, and it's too late, and the boy is already dead." She looked at me directly.

"That's the story. A man kills the one thing in the world he'd have died for, with his own hands, over two days, in front of everybody, and he only finds out what he's done at the very end. And the cure for it existed the entire time." "That's a hell of a bedtime story."
"They're all like that," she said. "That's the whole book. That's why it's a thousand years old."
And then she said the other thing, and I only understood it much later, and I'm putting it here where it happened rather than where it landed.

"There are two words," she said. "From much older than the book. Druj. It means the Lie. Not lying — not you saying you'd had four fights. The Lie. The thing that runs the wrong way underneath the world and looks completely convincing. And asha, which is the other one. The true order. What's actually the case."
"And?"
"And in the religion, the whole job of a life — the entire job — is you stand on the side of the true thing. That's it. That's all that's asked of anybody." "Even if it's terrible?"
"Especially then," said Parvaneh Ashkani. "It doesn't say anywhere that it's kind. It only says it's true."

She put the coffee in the bin without drinking it and went back down the corridor toward the walkway, and she didn't say the words again, ever, and she never explained them to me twice. I thought about it for the whole drive.
Not the two words. I filed those and they sat there like a stone in a shoe for months.

What I thought about was the medicine, and the king who delayed. That's the part that got me. Because that's not a story about a man who kills his son. Any fool can write that. That's a story about how the thing that would have saved him was sitting in a room the whole time, and it arrived, and it arrived at the wrong hour, and being late is the same as never for the one lying on the ground.
I remember thinking, on the Bishop Ford, going north past the exit: Well, I'm not late. I've got it in my hand.

I had it exactly backwards. I always did. She told me the whole thing straight out in a corridor in September and I heard a story about a man who was too slow, and it was a story about a man who was told the truth and preferred the other thing.
36. You Didn't Even Cry
Fight eleven. October. Down the shaft.
A man named Bo Threadgill, thirty-nine, out of Hammond, and he had a scar down the front of his throat from something that wasn't fighting.

Twenty-six minutes, and I'm going to give you all of it, because it is the last one where two men were doing something to each other rather than one man making a purchase. Minutes one to four. He was better than me and we both found out inside ninety seconds.

Threadgill fought out of a low crouch with his lead hand down around his belt, which looks like an invitation and is not, because a hand at the belt has further to travel and therefore comes up from underneath — from outside your vision — and you cannot see a punch that starts below your own eyeline. He hit me three times in the first two minutes with a left uppercut I never saw once. Not didn't pick up in time. Never saw. Three times, under the chin, straight up the middle. What an uppercut does that a hook doesn't is drive the head backward and up, which stretches everything down the front of the neck and slams the back of the skull onto the top of the spine, and after the third one my jaw felt loose in its hinges the way a gate is loose.

I put the jab in his face and he took it on the forehead on purpose, which is a professional's move — you eat the jab on the hardest part of your head, deliberately, because it costs you nothing and it costs the other man a hand.
By minute four I understood I was going to lose this, and I felt, God help me, relieved. Minutes four to nine. The brow.

He opened the right one at four minutes ten with a short left hook, and it did not open like a cut, it opened like a hem. That stitch line — twenty-two of them, twenty-two days old, taken out in a five-minute appointment in a room with a vinyl floor — let go along its whole length at once, and it took the tissue either side with it. So what I had was not a laceration. It was a flap: an inch and a half of eyebrow and the skin above it, hinged along the top, hanging.
I want to describe what that is from the inside, because it is the strangest physical sensation I have ever had, and I have had my jaw broken.

It's cold. That's the thing. Cold, in a warm place, and moving. There is a piece of you on the outside now, and it swings when you move, half a beat behind, and every time you turn your head you feel it go and then slap back against the wet.

And nothing can be done about it. There is no between. No round, no thirty seconds, no Denny with a thumb on my cheekbone and a number eleven blade. Vic stood at the edge of the circle with a tackle box he was not permitted to open until it was over, and he told me afterward that he had it on the floor and unlatched at minute five and then stood there with his hands at his sides for twenty-one more.

So I fought with my own face hanging off me, and a minute later I stopped being able to see out of that eye, and it was almost a mercy, because at least then I couldn't feel it in the light. Minutes nine to fourteen. I had the best five minutes of the whole run.
That's what I want on the record. Blind on the right, face open, thirteen months into this, and for five minutes down there I boxed the way I could box in 2006.
Because he came in. He'd smelled it, and men smell it, and he stopped being careful — and a careful man who stops being careful is a gift.

I turned everything a quarter to the left so the dead side pointed away and made him come round into the live one. I stopped throwing the right entirely. Jab, jab, hook off the jab. An old man's combination that every fighter alive sees coming and nobody can do anything about if the feet are right. I hit him with that hook eleven or twelve times in five minutes and by minute thirteen Bo Threadgill's left eye was closing and his mouth was open. And at thirteen forty I put him down.

Right hand over the top, on the temple — the only right I'd thrown in five minutes, which is exactly why it landed — and he went down on one knee in the black water with his bare hand flat on the concrete, breathing.
A hundred and forty men made a low noise off a curved ceiling. And there is no count.

Down there, when a man goes down, nothing happens. Nobody counts. Nobody comes in. It hangs there, two men in a room and one of them on a knee, and it is entirely up to the one standing whether he steps in and ends it. I stood over Bo Threadgill for about four seconds. And I didn't finish him.

I have never satisfactorily explained that to myself. I've offered myself two versions. Version one is decency: he was thirty-nine, he had a scar on his throat, he was on a knee in a hole in the ground, and something in me that was raised right would not do it.

Version two is the true one, and I know it's the true one because it arrived first, in about a fifth of a second, fully formed, with a reason already attached: If you stop it now, you don't get her. Minutes fourteen to twenty-one. He got up, and he had my number, and he made me pay the whole bill in one go.

At fourteen ten his thumb went into my left eye. Not on purpose — bare hands means fingers, and fingers in a small dark space means eyes, and everybody who has ever done this knows it and nobody has ever solved it. It went in at the inside corner, past the lid, and there is a noise your head makes at that moment which is not a noise at all, it's a white flash, and then the eye floods and shuts and stays shut. There was a bright orange smear across everything on that side for four days after, which I did not tell anybody about.

So: both gone. Right one blind under blood, left one blind under water and its own lid. Seven minutes of forearms up, chin behind them, staying in contact with him and reading him off the pressure on my arms the way you feel along a wall in a blackout.

He cracked the third and fourth ribs on the left at eighteen minutes with a right hand under the arm while I was tied up. A cracked rib announces itself immediately as a bright horizontal line about eight inches long that lights up on every single inhale for six weeks, and there is no way to fight without breathing, so you simply agree to be electrocuted forty times a minute until this is over.

At twenty minutes he took the top left canine out. Not chipped — out, the whole tooth with the root on it, and there was a sound conducted up through the jawbone into my ear like a fence post coming out of frozen ground, and then a hole my tongue found instantly and would not leave alone, hot and open and four times the size it turned out to be. I found that tooth on the floor afterward with the light of a phone. It's in a drawer and I don't know why.
Minutes twenty-one to twenty-six. The wall.

He put me on it at twenty-one and I stayed on it for five minutes, and there is nothing to describe except the arithmetic, so here's the arithmetic. A man who is not being counted, in a room with no rounds, against a target that cannot get off a wall, throws about one every six to nine seconds, because that is the rhythm of a tired man hitting something stationary. Five minutes is three hundred seconds. Call it forty. On top of the sixty or so before it.
And Ashkani's voice, which I had been carrying around for three weeks like a stone in a shoe: it isn't the one that puts you down, it's the nine hundred that didn't.
I remember thinking that on the wall, at about minute twenty-four, in the orange dark, in the middle of it. There they are.
And I remember one more thing, and this is the closest I ever came to stopping, and nobody has ever heard it.

Around minute twenty-five, with my back on wet concrete and my face hanging off me and a tooth somewhere on the floor and a man hitting me every seven seconds, I heard my own voice, very clear, from a long way inside, and it said: You could just sit down.
Not stay down. Sit down. Like a man at the end of a shift. And I said no.

Out loud, apparently. Threadgill heard it. He told Vic afterward that the old guy said no to somebody in the middle of the twenty-fifth minute, and that it put the wind up him worse than anything else that happened down there. Minute twenty-six. Left hook on the hinge of the jaw. I went down on my face in the water and I did not get up and the bell went.
VISIT NINE.

The kitchen. The four o'clock light — I want to say the light was right, but I don't trust myself on the light anymore. She was at the counter and she turned around. And she said: "You didn't even cry."

I have gone over this ten thousand times and I can tell you exactly how it sounded, which was: perfectly normal. Conversational. Not cruel in the delivery at all. She said it the way you'd say there's no milk. I said — I don't know what I said. Something.

And she said: "You didn't cry at the hospital and you didn't cry at Zaremba's and you stood there at Holy Cross with your hand on my back like a man at a bus stop and you didn't cry, and then you sat in that fucking chair for three years." And I said, "Nuala —" And she said, "Don't."

Thirty seconds. Then it was gone and I was on wet concrete with a hundred and forty men going round the walls and Vic's headlamp in my one working eye and his hands already in the tackle box, twenty-one minutes late.
Now here is where I have to be very careful, and it's the hardest bit of honesty in this whole account, so let me do it slowly.
Everybody who's heard this — both of them — has said the same thing, which is: that's your own guilt talking. That's not her. You put that in her mouth.
And I know. I know that's the obvious reading and it's probably true.
But I want to enter one thing into the record, one small thing, and then I'll shut up about it. Nobody knew.

I never told anybody that I didn't cry for my son. Not Denny. Not Colleen. Not one human being on this earth in seven years. It's the thing I put in chapter eleven and said I want it written down about, and the reason I said that is that it had never been out of me before, not once, in any form.

So either that sentence came from my own guilt, dressed up in my wife's voice, which is what any sensible person thinks — — or the room three hundred feet under the flats had finally got down far enough to reach the woman who actually knew me, and she had opened with the truest thing about me, first, the way she always did, because Nuala Deane did not do small talk and never in her life had she started with the keys.
She'd been asking about the keys for eight visits before this one.
She'd never once asked about the keys in her life without following it with something else.

I lay on the concrete with my face in four pieces and a tooth somewhere on the floor and I thought, for the first time since December: What if the nice one was the fake? And then I got up, because they need the floor.
37. Rehearsing Her
I spent November trying to fix her at home. It was the stupidest month of my life and I'd like it noted that it came from love.

The logic was clean. If she's built from parts — Ashkani's word, assembled — then the parts must still be in the house. Objects hold pieces. The smell of a coat holds a piece. So: gather the parts, rebuild her properly, in good light, sober, in a chair, without a hammer. Do it right, the way you'd restore something. And then next time I go down I'll have a good clean master copy in my hands and the damage can't get at it.
That was the plan. I actually wrote it on the back of an envelope. So I opened the house.

For twelve days I went into rooms I hadn't been in since 2017. I opened the bedroom door and took the bathrobe off the back of it and held it — and I was right, I was a man holding a bathrobe, and then what, and the answer is that you put it on the bed and you stand there.

I got out everything. The four hundred and eleven photographs. Her books, which she'd read in the bath so half of them are swollen. Her handwriting: shopping lists, a birthday card, three years of a work diary with nothing in it but shift times and the initials of people she liked and didn't. The green jacket. The elastic from the plastic bag with the case number on it.
And I sat in the front room with all of it laid out and I worked. Hours a night. Trying to run her in my head, deliberately, like a film. Trying to make her turn around.
Here's what happened, and this is the part nobody warned me about and I'd have paid a lot for the warning.
Every time I did it, she got a little more like the kitchen version.

I'd start with something specific — an argument we had in a Hyundai outside her mother's house in 2016 about her brother — and about six seconds in, the Nuala doing the arguing would soften. Her sentences would get shorter. She'd stop landing on me and start drifting. The vicious, fast, mean, funny thing that could take the roof off a room kept sliding, every session, toward a nice woman in a cardigan in nice light who was patient with me.
Because I was building her out of what I had. And what I had was the kitchen version, nine times reinforced, run into the ground like a footpath across a lawn.
You understand what I was doing? I was going into the vault every night with the forgery in my hand and using it as the reference.

By about the twentieth of November I could not get her to say anything unkind to me. Not one thing. And this is a woman who once told me, in a car, in traffic, that I had "the emotional range of a parking meter," and I could no longer make her say it. I could recite the sentence — I've got the words, the words are here on this page — but I could not get her to say it. The words came out flat, in my voice, like a man reading a card.
I had a woman in my head who agreed with me about everything and forgave me for all of it and stood in nice light asking about her keys.

And it was around the twenty-second, at about two in the morning, with the whole house open and every light on and my dead wife's belongings covering two rooms, that I sat down on the stairs and understood the actual shape of what I'd done. It's not that I lost her.
It's that I replaced her with somebody who was easier to be married to.

Nine times. In a barn, in a scrap yard, in a truck bay, in a room under the flats. Every single visit I had gone down there and come back up with a version of Nuala Deane that was very slightly warmer, softer, more forgiving, less there — and I had been calling that a miracle.
And there is only one way that keeps happening in one direction. Somebody in there was choosing.
I put everything back. Took me two days. Bathrobe on the door. Photographs in the box. And I called Gaz Tunney and got on the December card and did not sleep well for the rest of the month.
38. Where's My Bag

Fight twelve. December, down the shaft, and it was fifty-four degrees down there like it is every day of the year, and up top it was nine with the wind off the lake, and the difference made the shaft breathe.
A man named Curtis Wardell, forty-five, exactly my age, which felt like a joke somebody was making at my expense. Twenty-two minutes. Two things worth recording.

The first is that I could not remember, at any point during that fight, how long it had been going. Not roughly. At all. There was no sense of elapsed time whatsoever — no we must be about ten minutes in — and it turns out that keeping a running count of how long a thing has been happening is a job that something in your head does for you, quietly, free, your entire life, and when it stops doing it you are simply in a permanent now with no idea how you got there or how long you've been. It's not frightening at the time. That's the trouble with all of it. It's only frightening afterward, when you're describing it. The second is that I cut him.

I want to put this down because it's the last time in my life I did something in a fight that a coach would have recognized. Wardell had a scar on the outer edge of his right eye, an old one, pale, running down and out. And I saw it in the sodium in the fourth minute and thirty-four years of training said there, and I put the jab on it — not the hook, the jab, the ruler, over and over, thirty or forty times on one square inch of a man's face — and at minute nine it came apart like wet paper and blinded him on that side, and I walked him into the wall with it and hit him nine times in a row. He went down. He got up.

That's the thing about the room. Getting up is the only thing there is to do down there. Nobody stops it. So Curtis Wardell got up blind on one side and I did it again, and he went down, and he got up, and I remember thinking, distantly, in an admiring sort of way: You poor bastard, you're in the same business I am.

Because he was. Of course he was. Nobody comes three hundred feet down a shaft in December for twelve hundred dollars. Everybody in that room was buying something and none of us ever said one word about it to each other. A hundred and forty men in a hole under the city, all of us with a reason, and the whole culture of the place was that you never, ever asked, which I used to think was hardness and I now understand was the last shred of decency any of us had left.
He put me down at twenty-two with a right hand that I honestly think was thrown at random.
VISIT TEN.
The kitchen. Grayer than it should be. Colder.
She wasn't at the counter. She was standing in the doorway that goes through to the hall.
That's new. In nine visits she had never once been anywhere but the counter.
And she said, one sentence, flat, level, no rise in the middle: "Sean, where's my bag." That's it. That's the whole visit. Maybe six seconds.
I came round on the concrete and I said out loud, to a room of a hundred and forty men, "It's in the car." Vic said, "What's in the car?" I said, "Nothing."

And I lay there with my ribs going and one eye and a headache with a taste to it, and I thought about a printed sheet from the Illinois State Police that had been folded along the same three creases for four and a half years in the middle drawer of a sideboard twelve feet from where I sleep. One (1) suitcase, hardshell, blue, approx. 26 in. One (1) duffel bag, canvas, olive.
And the story came, right on time, three seconds, no effort, no discomfort at all: Bernie's move.

But this time — and this is the only credit I will ever take in this entire account — this time, some flat unimpressed part of me that has never once been listened to said, from a long way off, in a voice with absolutely nothing in it: Bernie moved in 2019, Sean. And I said, out loud, on the floor, in the orange dark: "Shut up."
39. The Worst Thing I Ever Did
His name was Marek Sowinski and he was nineteen years old.

I'd seen him twice in the gallery, standing at the back where the new ones stand, and I'd asked Gaz about him, and Gaz said he was a Polish kid out of Portage Park, that he'd had a few in the truck bay, that he was an animal, that he'd knocked out a thirty-two-year-old in ninety seconds in October, and that he was nineteen and had never been down the shaft.
"He's got no experience," Gaz said. "He's got the other thing." "What's the other thing?"
"He doesn't stop," said Gaz Tunney. "You know. Some of them just don't have the part that stops." I said: "Put me in with him."
Gaz said: "Sean. He's twenty-seven years younger than you and he's got two hands and you've got a face like a road accident. That's not a fight, that's a —"

And then Gaz Tunney, five foot six, quarter-zip, phone in each hand, a man who had never in his life told anybody to do anything, stopped, and did not finish the sentence. "January fourteenth," he said.
That's what I asked for. That's what I got. And that's not the worst thing I did, that's just the arrangement. Here's the worst thing I did.

On the second of January, in the afternoon, I drove up to Portage Park and I found the kid at a gym on Milwaukee, and I waited outside in the truck until he came out with a bag over his shoulder and earbuds in, and I got out and said his name.

He knew who I was. That's the first thing. He took the earbuds out and his whole face changed and he said, "You're Vardy." Nineteen years old, and somewhere in his life there'd been a card at the Aragon on a screen, or an uncle who'd told him, and here was the actual man on a sidewalk on Milwaukee Avenue with a dropped cheek and two brows made of scar. "I want to buy you a coffee," I said. We sat in a Dunkin' for fifty minutes.

He was — and I want this in, because it matters, because if he'd been a thug this would be a much easier chapter to write — he was a sweet kid. Big, thick-necked, with a gap in his teeth and a laugh that came too easy, and he called me sir twice before I got him to stop, and he told me about his mother's back and the shift he worked at a distribution center in Franklin Park and about a girl who had recently made a decision he was still processing. He asked me about the Aragon. He asked what it was like to be on television.
And then he asked me, shy, the way you ask a man you admire, whether I had any advice. And I gave him some.
I said: forget the body. Everybody your age goes to the body because it feels solid and it makes a noise. Body work wins you rounds and there aren't any rounds down there. Go to the head.

I said: the brow ridge is where you start. Everybody thinks you go to the chin. The chin ends it, but the brows open it, and once a man's got blood in his eye you can do whatever you like. And on an older fighter the brows are already scar — there's no skin left in them, it's all patch, and a patch doesn't stretch, so it parts on the first good one.

I said: the temple. Flat of the fist won't do it, you'll break your hand on the top of the skull. It's the front two knuckles, straight through the wrist, on the flat spot in front of the ear. That one turns the head around its own axis and that's the one that puts a man out.
I said: when he's against the wall and he's holding you, don't stand off. Let him hold you. Breathe. And then start again. Nobody's going to stop you.

I said: and if he goes down and gets up, and goes down and gets up, don't back off out of respect. That's the mistake everybody makes the first time. You back off, you let him gather, and the whole thing goes another twenty minutes and you both get wrecked. If a man wants to keep getting up, the kindest thing on this earth is to put him all the way out.
And Marek Sowinski, nineteen years old, wrote it in his phone. He wrote it in his phone.

And then he thanked me — he thanked me, he shook my hand with both of his — and he said, "I got a guy on the fourteenth, down the tunnel, my first one down there," and I said, "Yeah, I heard," and he said, "You know who it is?"
And I said, "No." That's it. That's the worst thing I've ever done.

I have thought about it more than I have thought about the visits, more than I have thought about Fionn, more than I have thought about anything, and I want to lay out precisely what it consists of, because the surface of it isn't the crime. The surface is: a man arranged his own beating. The crime underneath is:

I took a nineteen-year-old boy with a laugh that came too easy and a mother with a bad back, and I made him the instrument. I stood on a sidewalk on Milwaukee Avenue and I picked him up and turned him into a tool for getting something I wanted. I gave him a technical education in how to destroy a specific human face, which was mine, so that on the fourteenth of January he would be efficient about it, and I did not tell him.

Because he would have said no. That's the whole point. That kid would have said no in a heartbeat, he'd have said I'm not doing that, that's fucked up, he'd have been appalled — nineteen years old and more decent in one afternoon than I'd been in fourteen months — and I knew that, and so I withheld the one piece of information that would have let him choose.
I took his consent off him and I did it in a Dunkin' with a coffee.

And there's an after. That's the part people don't get to when they're being generous with me. It isn't that I used him for an evening. It's that whatever came of the fourteenth of January, he was going to have to carry it, at nineteen, for sixty years, and I set that up, deliberately, with technical advice, in a doughnut shop, from a man he'd watched on television as a child.
I paid for his coffee. He said thanks. I remember I said, "Keep your hands up," and he laughed.

You want to know what a transgression actually is? Everybody thinks it's the blood. It's not the blood. I have described more damage in this book than most people see in a lifetime and none of it is transgressive, it's just meat, it's just what happens when bone meets bone at speed.
A transgression is a man on a sidewalk in Portage Park in January, being kind, being generous with his time, giving a boy the best technical advice he has, and knowing exactly what he's doing.
40. Eleven Seconds
Fight thirteen. The sixth of January, truck bay, Torrence.

I could not wait twelve days. That's all this chapter is. The fourteenth was arranged, everything was in place, the kid had it written in his phone, and I could not get from the second of January to the fourteenth of January without something in between, so I took a fight on the sixth in the truck bay off Torrence for four hundred dollars against a man whose name I did not catch and have never learned.

Four hundred. I'd been getting twelve hundred down the shaft. I took four hundred to fight a stranger in a truck bay eight days before the biggest beating of my life, and if you want the medical chart of what I had become by January of 2023, that transaction is the chart.
He was young and he was terrible and he hit like a door and it took him fourteen minutes.

The damage: nothing new. That's what I remember about it. There was nothing left to break for the first time — every structure in my face had already been broken and healed wrong, so it all just went again along the old lines, brows, nose, the rim, the arch, like a man kicking in a door that's already off its hinges. Vic wasn't there. Somebody's brother-in-law put superglue in the right brow, which Denny had told me not to let happen, and which fused the flap down crooked and is the reason my right eyebrow now sits about four millimeters higher than the left and gives me, according to my sister, a permanent expression of mild surprise. I went down at fourteen minutes.
VISIT ELEVEN.

Here is all of it. I'm not editing. — light. Not four o'clock. Not any hour. — the counter. Not the whole counter. A corner of it, and the edge of the sink, and nothing behind it, no window, no wall, just an absence where the rest of the kitchen should be, and I could not look at it directly, the way you can't look at the middle of your own eye. — blue. The cardigan, or the color of it, without a shape. — the hair elastic. That was clear. The elastic on her wrist, and the two little marks it makes in the skin, and the small dark hairs caught in it. Very clear. Clearer than anything.

— a sound like the start of my name. Not my name. The shape a mouth makes going into it. — hook. The word hook, on its own, with no sentence around it. — and something turning. Something in the room turned away from me, or turned toward me, I could not tell which, and there was no face on it either way.
Eleven seconds. Vic's brother-in-law counted, later, when I asked, because he'd noticed me go still. Eleven seconds.

I came round on the concrete of a truck bay off Torrence Avenue with a mouthful of my own blood and a superglued eyebrow, and I lay there, and the propane heaters were roaring at the ceiling doing nothing at floor level, and I understood something with total clarity for the first time since a VFW hall in Cicero thirteen months earlier. She was nearly gone.

Not the connection was bad. Not the venue. I had run out of the thing. I had gone into the drawer eleven times and there wasn't much in the drawer anymore, and what was left was an elastic and the word hook.

And a normal man — and I want to make sure you understand that I know what a normal man does here, I've always known, I have never at any point in this been confused about what the correct action was — a normal man gets up off that floor and goes home and never does it again, and spends the rest of his life protecting the eleven seconds he's got left. I got up off that floor and thought: Then the fourteenth has to be the big one.

Because there was one thing left in the account and I was going to spend all of it at once, on the largest purchase available, in the deepest room in the city, against a nineteen-year-old boy I had personally trained.
I want to be clear that this was not despair. People assume despair. Despair would be a comfort to me now.
It was planning. It was the same feeling as a man booking a flight.
