41. The Corridor
The fourteenth of January, 2023. Here's the day.

I woke at six on the couch in the front room, because that's where I sleep, all nights, four years and change of nights, and the first thing I did was lie there for a quarter of an hour trying to establish what day it was, which by January was simply part of waking up, like a piss.

Then the inventory. You do it lying down, before you move, because if you do it standing you'll fall over and then you've learned nothing. Ribs: three and four on the left, eight days out, sharp on the inhale, fine on the exhale, so breathe shallow and don't laugh. Right hand: the two middle knuckles swollen and hot, some crap in there from the sixth, grip about seventy percent. Left hand: the crooked one, cold-ache, fine. Neck: the thing behind the left ear that never came back after Duca, so no looking left, so the world stays a half-circle. Right eye: fine. Left eye: the orange smear from Threadgill's thumb, mostly gone, some flicker at the outside edge like something moving that isn't. Head: taste behind the left eye. Present. Constant. Metal, and slightly sweet, like blood and a battery. Then I got up and I didn't fall over, so: a good day. Breakfast. Four eggs, dry toast, no coffee, which is a rule I've had since 2003 — no caffeine on a fight day, because caffeine puts your heart at a hundred before you've done anything and then you've got nowhere to go. Also I drank a liter of water at eight and a liter at noon and nothing after two, because a dehydrated brain sits lower in the skull and has further to travel before it hits the wall, and that is not a metaphor, that's the actual mechanism, and every fighter in the world dries himself out to make weight and every one of them is buying a slightly worse concussion.

I hydrated. I want that in the record. I did the one thing that was good for me, on that day, out of thirty-four years of habit, like a man polishing the shoes he's going to be buried in. Two in the afternoon. I cut my nails. Bare hands, and a nail catches and tears off backward and then you've got a finger you can't use. Half past two. I shaved the eyebrows down with a beard trimmer. Everybody thinks that's for the look. It's so hair doesn't get carried into the cut, which is how a brow goes septic. Three. I greased my face. Vaseline, heavy, on both brows, the nose, the cheekbones, worked in with two fingers, and the point of it is that a fist slides off grease and grabs on dry skin, and every fraction of a second of slide is force that goes past you instead of into you. I did it standing at the bathroom mirror on Baltimore Avenue with the light on, and I looked at the face while I did it: the dropped right cheek, the stepped rim over the left eye, the nose flat and off-center, the right brow four millimeters high courtesy of a man's brother-in-law and a tube of superglue, the gap on the top left where the canine was. Forty-six years old. I said out loud, to the mirror: "You handsome bastard." Four. I sat in the front room with the television on and the sound down and I did not think about anything at all for two hours, and that is the truth, and if you've never had a fight day you won't believe it, and if you have you'll know exactly what I'm describing. The whole day is a corridor. You're not nervous. Nervous ended around 1994. You're just going along it. Six. Boots. Not shoes — work boots, laced tight to the top, because that floor is running with water and a man who slips down there gets kicked in the head by accident by his own opponent, which I have seen. Two pairs of socks. Track pants. A T-shirt I didn't care about, which is a sentence with a lot in it. Half past six. Wrapped my own hands. Bare fight, so it's not padding, it's a wrist strap — two figure-eights around the wrist and the base of the thumb and nothing over the knuckles, and it's the only thing standing between you and your wrist folding backward on the first good shot. I've had Denny Fewster wrap my hands since 1988. I did it myself at the kitchen table with the roll in my teeth and I did it badly. Twenty to seven. I stood in the dining room in front of the sideboard for about four minutes. I didn't open it.

I want to say that plainly. On the last day, standing in front of the drawer that had the answer in it, with all the time in the world, I did not open it, and there was no drama in the not-opening, there wasn't a struggle, I did not feel my hand go toward the handle. I stood there the way you stand in front of a bookshelf. And then I went and got my keys off the hook.

Off the hook. Where they live. Where they have always fucking lived. Seven. I called Colleen in Naperville and talked to her for twenty minutes about her boy's hockey and a problem she was having with a neighbor's tree, and I said the right things in the right gaps, and at the end she said, "Sean, are you eating?" and I said, "Constantly," and she said, "You sound flat," and I said, "It's the phone," and she said, "Okay. Love you, dummy," and I said, "Love you," and hung up.

That's the last conversation I had with anybody in my family in the old way. I didn't know it. Nobody ever knows it. But if you'd told me, I wouldn't have changed a word of it, and I'd like credit for that, because it was a good one. A tree and some hockey. That's the right way to go out. Half past eight. I drove down to the flats and parked on the service road and walked four hundred yards along a fence with the weeds dead and stiff with frost, and I went through the gate with the wrong padlock, and I stood in a steel headhouse with no windows, and six of us got into a cage, and a man up top pulled a lever. Ninety seconds.
The square of orange sky got smaller like something being closed.
42. The Bell
Fight fourteen. He saw me from across the gallery and his face fell open.

That's the first thing. Before anything else, I want it recorded that Marek Sowinski, nineteen years old, standing in an orange room three hundred feet under Illinois with his hands already wrapped, looked across at the man he was fighting and understood in about a second and a half what had been done to him in a Dunkin' on Milwaukee Avenue twelve days earlier, and the look on his face was not anger. It was shame. He was ashamed. He looked at the floor.

He came over. There were men between us and he came through them and he stood in front of me and he said, quietly, so nobody else could hear it: "Sir — I didn't know it was you." "I know." "I can't —" "You can."
"No, I'm gonna —" He was working very hard. Nineteen. "I'm gonna tell them I'm out. I'll pay them back the —"
And I leaned in, close to his ear, and I said the thing that I will be paying for after everything else in this book has been forgiven.

I said: "Marek. I asked for you. I picked you out. If you walk up that shaft I'll be down here next month with somebody worse, and he won't be any good, and he'll take four times as long, and that'll be on you too."
I let him stand there with that for a second and then I put my hand on the back of his neck like a man being kind and I said:
"Front two knuckles. Flat spot in front of the ear. You wrote it down." The bell went. The first four minutes. He wouldn't fight.

I mean it literally — he came out and he circled and he threw a jab at my shoulder, at my shoulder, deliberately wide, three or four times, and behind him the room started to make a noise, and the noise that a hundred and forty men make in a wet concrete tube when they think they're being cheated is not something you want directed at a nineteen-year-old.
So I hit him.

I want to be honest about this: I hit that boy in the mouth as hard as I have ever hit anything in my life. Right hand, bare, no give in it, straight through the wrist, and it went through his upper lip and put it onto his teeth and split it from the middle of the lip up into the nostril, so that afterward he had a flap and you could see his gum through his own face when he breathed. I hit him to make him fight me. That's a thing I did.

He tasted it and something went across his eyes and the sweet kid from the doughnut shop stepped out of the way for the animal, which was the entire reason I'd chosen him. Minutes four to nine. He put me on the wall.

He was two hundred and five pounds of nineteen and he walked me back across the wet floor like a man moving a wardrobe, and my shoulder blades went onto the concrete, and there was the seep coming down between my shirt and the wall, cold, running down into my waistband, which is a detail I'd forgotten about until just now.
And then he went to the brows, exactly the way I'd taught him, exactly.

Left brow first. Four short right hands from close, no windup, elbow tight, and on the third one it parted — that's the word, it doesn't split, there's no skin left to split, the scar just comes open along its length like a seam letting go — and I felt the heat go across and then the wet, and then the left side of the world shut down.

Right brow, second, and the superglue from the sixth of January made it worse, exactly as Denny said it would, because glue holds the top edge fast so all the movement goes into the tissue underneath and it tears wider than a stitch line would. That one opened about two inches, from the outer end almost to the bridge, and it went so deep that afterward Vic said he could see the bone the whole length of it.
And that was it for seeing. Nine minutes in, both eyes gone under blood, and no rounds, so no wiping. Minutes nine to sixteen. The blind stretch.
Here's what fighting blind is, when there is no bell coming and no corner and no one to stop it.

You hold your forearms up in a vee in front of your face and you keep your chin behind them and you listen. Not for sound — the room's a murmur, it's all one noise — for the small changes in weight against your arms. A man about to throw has to load, and loading moves his weight, and if any part of him is touching any part of you, you feel it a fraction before it happens. So you keep contact. That's the whole trade. Forearm against forearm, glove-less wrist against his elbow, staying in touch with him the way a blind man stays in touch with a wall.
He hit me between forty and fifty times in those seven minutes.

He hit the top of my head twice, ducking, and broke his own right hand. I heard it. And to his credit and to my everlasting sorrow he did not stop, he just started using the left, which is what I would have told him to do if I'd thought of it, and I hadn't, and he worked it out on his own, and I remember being proud of him.

Somewhere in there the nose went for the last time and this time it went with a different sound, softer, because there wasn't much bone left in it to break, it was mostly cartilage and old repairs, and after that I could not get air through it at all and I was breathing entirely through a mouth that was full of blood, which is a thing you can do for a surprisingly long time and which I do not recommend.

Somewhere in there he hit me on the left orbital rim, on the step, on the ledge that Ashkani said had set wrong, and it came apart along the old fracture, and I heard the crunch through the bone of my skull, and my left eye — which was already blind under blood — dropped, physically, into the socket, so that when the swelling later went down enough for me to see out of it, everything on that side was about an inch lower than it should have been and did not line up with the other one, and never has since.

Somewhere in there something happened to my right ear. I don't know what. Vic says it was folded. The ear's not the same shape now, it's got a ridge across the top and a solid feel to it like a piece of shell, and Denny would have drained it, and Denny wasn't there.

And somewhere in there, at about minute fourteen, in the middle of all of it, standing blind against a wet wall with my arms up, taking a shot every eight or nine seconds from a nineteen-year-old with a broken hand, I felt a thing I have never told anybody and am telling you. I felt comfortable.

Not brave. Not resigned. Comfortable, the way you are in a chair that fits. My head was completely empty. Not confused — empty, in the good way, in the 1988-boiler-room way. There was no house. There was no drawer. There was no inventory sheet folded in three. There was no chair with the sound down and no hedge and no small back bedroom I don't go in. There was a wall behind me and a boy in front of me and the problem of him, and that was the entire contents of the universe, and I want to tell you honestly that those were the best seven minutes I'd had since March of 2015. That's what I was buying. Not just her. That. Minute sixteen. He put me down for the first time.

Left hook, blind side, on the hinge of the jaw. I went down in the way where you don't put your hands out, and my face went into the wet concrete, and I lay there in the black water with my cheek on it and I could taste the floor, that mineral wet-coin taste, mixed with mine. The room went quiet, or quieter. And I got up.

Nobody counts down there. There's no reason to get up down there except that you want to. I want you to sit with that. Every other time in my life that I've got up off a floor, there was a man over me counting, and a rule, and the whole architecture of the sport saying here is your chance, take it or don't. Down there it is just a man on the ground deciding, in front of a hundred and forty people, all on his own, with no clock, whether to stand back up into it. I decided eleven times.
I'm going to say that once and not dress it up. Between minute sixteen and minute thirty-one, Marek Sowinski put me down eleven times and I got up eleven times.

The boy was crying by about the seventh. I know because I heard it in his breathing, close, in the clinch, that catch. He was hitting me and crying. Nineteen. And twice he said, "Stay down," in the clinch, right in my ear, quietly, a plea, and the second time he said "please," and I said — and this is the last coherent sentence I said as the man I used to be — I said: "Sorry, kid. You're the only one still working."

Minute thirty-one. He hit me on the temple. Flat spot in front of the ear. Front two knuckles, straight through the wrist, left hand, because the right was broken. Exactly where I told him. Exactly how.

And thirty-four years, and nineteen and four and one, and a boiler room on 106th Street, and a brown chair with a hostage in it, and eleven days of a boy called Fionn, and four hundred and eleven photographs, and a hedge taller than a window, and a drawer with a sheet of paper folded in three, all of it, everything, went out like a lightbulb. The bell went. And I was in the kitchen.
43. The Accurate Woman
It was night.

That's the first thing that was wrong, and I knew it before I knew anything else, the way you know a wrong note before you know the tune. There was no gold coming in over the sink. The window over the sink was black and it had the room in it, doubled, the way a kitchen window does after dark, and the overhead was on — the ugly one, the ceiling fixture with the two bulbs and the dead moths in it that we said for four years we were going to replace. The clock on the stove said 11:40.

And it was cold in there, actually cold, because the back door was open about a foot with the storm door shut behind it, which is what she did when she'd burned something, and there was that smell, scorched pan, and the extractor was running. And she was in the doorway to the hall with a coat on.
Not the cardigan. A coat, buttoned, and boots, and her hair was down, and she had a canvas duffel over her shoulder, olive, and a hardshell case in her other hand, blue, twenty-six inches.
And she was thirty-eight and she was furious and she looked like herself.

I want to try to explain what that was like and I don't have the equipment. It's like this. Imagine you have looked at a photograph of somebody every day for a year and then you see the person. And the person's face moves. Everything in a photograph is a decision that got made once and stuck. A real face is making decisions constantly, forty a second, and every one of them is information, and you can't imagine that. You can't build that. It doesn't matter how good your workshop is.

She was making decisions with her face at me. She was doing the thing with her jaw. She was breathing hard through her nose because she'd been shouting and had stopped shouting about ninety seconds ago and was now at the part after shouting, which is worse, which is the part where the voice goes quiet and level and reasonable and she takes you apart with her hands in her pockets. And she said: "I'm not doing this anymore, Sean."
That's what she said. That's what she actually said, on the fourth of November, 2017, at twenty to twelve at night, in our kitchen, with the storm door shut and a burnt pan in the sink.

And then the rest of it came. All of it. In order. In her voice, at her speed, with the sentences going up in the middle, landing on me every time, and I'm going to put down what I've got and I'm not going to soften it, because there's no point to any of this if I soften it now.

She said: "Three years. Three years, and I have done every single thing they tell you to do. I got us into the group. I got us to Dr. Mahaffey. I made the appointments, I drove us there, I paid for it, I did all the talking in the room, and you sat there like a coat on a chair." She said: "You didn't cry."

There it is. There it is, from a woman I have not been able to hear properly in six years, and I had it in a barn in October, in her mouth, thirty seconds of it, and I told myself it was my own guilt in a wig.

She said: "He was eleven days old and you didn't make a sound, and I thought, okay, that's shock, that's the man, he'll come round. And then it was a year. And then it was two. And in the second year I stopped grieving my son because I was too busy being married to a fucking piece of furniture."

She said: "Do you know what I do at work? Do you know what I actually do, all day, in the building where he died? I put my hands on people's chests and I keep them breathing. That's the job. And I come home to this house, and there's a man in a chair with the sound down, and I can't — Sean, I can't put my hands on you. There's nothing there to press on."

She said: "And the worst of it, the thing I can't get past, is that you're not even sad. If you were sad I'd have stayed. I'd have stayed forever with a sad man. You're not sad. You're gone. You went out and you left the house running."
And I said something. I have this. I have my own voice in it and I'd give anything not to. I said: "Where are you going to go?"

That's what I said. Not don't. Not I'm sorry. Not I'll do anything. My wife of four years stood in a doorway with two bags and told me she was leaving and I asked her about logistics. And she laughed. Once. No humor in it at all. She said: "Bernie's." She said: "I'll come for the rest when you're at work."

And then she stopped, in the doorway, with the duffel on her shoulder, and something went across her face — and I have gone through this frame by frame ten thousand times and I still don't know what it was, whether it was one more chance or just the pause a person takes before a hard door — and she said, in a completely different voice, a small one: "Sean. Say something."

And that's the shape of the woman I was married to. That's her. Right there, in one sentence, the whole of her: she comes at you with everything, she takes the roof off the room, she leaves you nothing to stand on — and then she stops in the doorway with her bags in her hands and gives you one more, because she can't help it, because she was the softest person I ever met underneath all that speed, and she was standing there at twenty to twelve at night waiting for me to open my mouth. And I want to tell you what I said.
I want to tell you what I said more than I have ever wanted anything, and I'm going to have to tell you in the next chapter that I don't know, and I'd rather cut my hands off.
But before that, understand what had just happened to me. Understand what the room three hundred feet under Illinois had actually just handed me, at the cost of everything I own. It was all a lie.

The kitchen with the four o'clock gold coming in over the sink. The blue cardigan with the pilled elbows. The hair up in the elastic. The flowers with the ends cut on the diagonal. The little green mess on the counter. The laugh — that laugh, the head going back an inch, the best four minutes of my adult life — Sean, did you move my keys? There is no such afternoon.

I have looked for it since. I've been through all four hundred and eleven photographs and I've asked her sister and I've asked my own sister and there is no cardigan. She didn't own a blue cardigan. I have described that cardigan to two people who knew her for thirty-eight years and both of them said, gently, no.

It's an assembly. It's a kitchen from some other day and a light from some other year and a garment from God knows where and a woman built out of everything I needed her to be — soft, patient, unhurried, forgiving, standing at a counter in nice light, asking me about her keys. Not angry. Never once angry. Not leaving. Never once leaving.

I built her. I started building her in a funeral home on the ninth of November, 2017, and I worked on her for four years without knowing it, every day, quietly, the way the body lays down scar over something it can't fix — and then I took her down a hole in the ground eleven times and finished her.

And then on the fourteenth of January, 2023, a nineteen-year-old boy I trained myself hit me on the flat spot in front of the ear with his front two knuckles, and knocked the whole thing down, and underneath it, standing in a doorway at twenty to twelve at night with a bag on her shoulder, furious, breathing hard, alive — there she was.
The real one. The accurate one. The last thing on this earth I wanted.
Truth. That's what the word means. Asha. She said it to me in a corridor with a coffee in her hand and I thought it was a nice thing about a religion.
It doesn't say anywhere that it's kind. It only says it's true.
44. The Eleven Minutes
The visit ended at say something. Not faded. Ended. Like film running out.

I woke up eleven days later in a bed on the sixth floor at Christ with a tube in my nose, which is a hell of a place to wake up when your nose is the thing that's broken, and the first coherent thought I had in 2023 was that I needed to get back into that kitchen and find out what I said.
That's the whole of the rest of my life, that sentence. Everything from here is just the paperwork.

Let me set out what I know, because it's all I've got, and God knows I've had time. Known. She was in the doorway with two bags at 11:40 p.m. The clock on the stove said it and I saw it and the stove clock ran four minutes fast, which I know because I set it, so call it 11:36 real. Known. The crash was logged at 11:53 p.m. Bishop Ford northbound, wet road, no impairment, no braking, a single vehicle and a barrier. That's on the report in the manila envelope and it's the one number in this whole business that nobody made up. Known. From my driveway on Baltimore Avenue to the point of impact is nine minutes at that hour. I have driven it. I have driven it more times than a sane man would. Nine minutes, at that hour, at the speed she drove, which was fast.

So: 11:36 in the doorway. 11:44 in the car, at the latest, to be dead at 11:53. Eight minutes. Somewhere between eight and eleven minutes, depending on the stove clock and the traffic and how honest I'm being on any given day. Call it the eleven, because I've called it the eleven for two years now and I'm not changing it. It's got eleven days of Fionn in it and eleven visits in it and eleven times I got up off a wet floor, and if there's one thing this whole account has taught me it's that a man will make anything mean anything. Eleven minutes between my wife saying Sean, say something and my wife driving away from this house for the last time. And I do not have them.

I want to be exact about the nature of the not-having, because it's not like forgetting where you put a thing. When you've forgotten something ordinary there's a shape to it, there's a hole with edges, you can feel around the rim of it and go it was something to do with the garage. This isn't that. Where those eleven minutes should be there is no rim. There's no edge to feel for. The tape says say something and then it says nothing, and it doesn't say nothing in a way that indicates something is missing. It's smooth.
And here's the thing that I have to live in now, so you might as well come in and have a look around:

I had it once. That's the part. I had those eleven minutes. On the fifth of November, 2017, and on the sixth, and through that whole first winter, whatever happened in this kitchen between say something and the sound of her car was in my head like everything else, in pieces, on shelves, retrievable. And I never went and got it.

For four years I did not open that drawer, and I did not open the other drawer, and I sat in a chair with the sound down and let a construction go up over the top of it like ivy over a wall. And then I took what was left of it down a shaft in the ground eleven times and ran it through the worst workshop a human being can build, and I came back up each time with a nice woman in a cardigan asking me about her keys.
It's gone. There is no copy. Ashkani said it and she was right and she was gentle about it and I've never forgiven her for either.
So here are the things I will not know until I die, and I'd like to list them, because listing them is the only operation I can still perform on them. Did I follow her out?
Did I stand in the kitchen? Did I sit down? Did I put the television on? Is that what I did — is there a version where a woman puts two bags in a car in the dark while her husband watches a program?

Did I say something? I asked her where she was going. That was 11:38. In the eleven minutes did I find anything better? Did I get up out of it, finally, for one minute, at the very end, four years too late — did I say don't, did I say I'm sorry, did I say I did love him, Nuala, I loved him, I just couldn't find where I'd put it — Did I put my hands on her?

I have to write that down because I think it every day. Not because there's evidence for it. Because there's no evidence against it, and after everything I've told you in this book about what I'm prepared to do to get what I want, I am not in a position to be certain about my own conduct in a room I can't remember being in. And two things sit on the table and neither will move. The first is Mrs. Zabrocki. Eighty-one, next door, up at all hours. She told the trooper — it's in the report, one line, neighbor reports hearing storm door twice — that she heard our storm door bang twice that night. Twice.

Twice means somebody went out and came back. Or somebody went out after somebody. Or she went out, and came back in for something, and went out again. Three readings and I have run them for two years and they will not resolve, and Mrs. Zabrocki died in 2020, and she was eighty-one, and she was watching a program with the sound up, and the trooper wrote one line.

The second is the keys. Every visit. Every single one, all twelve — no, eleven, because the twelfth was the true one and the keys weren't in it at all. Eleven times out of eleven, that woman in the four o'clock light turned around and asked me about her keys, and said they weren't on the hook.
Now. When I thought it was her, I thought it was nothing. It was the keys, it was our joke, it was the thing we said for four years, it was as ordinary as the coffee.
But it isn't her. I know that now. It's a construction, and I built it, and here's what I have learned about the things I build: Nothing in it is random.
Every part of that kitchen came from somewhere. The light came from an afternoon. The counter came from a counter. Even the cardigan came from something, some garment on some woman on some day.

So the sentence came from somewhere too. That sentence — the only one that survived all eleven passes, the last thing standing in the rubble when everything else had gone down to an elastic and the word hook — that sentence was made out of something.
And I have to ask: what does a man do, at twenty to twelve at night, when his wife is standing in a doorway with two bags?
There's a hook by that back door. I put it up in 2014. Her keys lived on it and mine live on it and mine are on it right now, I can see them from where I'm sitting.
Did I take her keys off her?

Did I stand between my wife and the door with her keys in my fist for eleven minutes? Is that what it was? Is that the load-bearing thing at the bottom of it — did I hold her here, arguing, for eleven minutes, in a house she was trying to leave, and then give them back, and did she go out of here so angry, so late, so done with me, that she drove onto a wet expressway at eleven fifty at night and didn't brake?
Or is the hook just a hook, and the keys are just the keys, and my brain grabbed the nearest domestic object to build a sentence out of, the way it grabbed a cardigan?
Both of those are completely consistent with every fact available to me. Both of them will be completely consistent with every fact available to me on the day I die.

I destroyed the witness. That's what I did. I sat in a chair for four years and let the file rot and then I went down a hole eleven times and burned what was left, and the witness — the only one, the only human being on this earth who was in that kitchen and could tell me what kind of man I was in it — was me.
And I'd like to tell you that this is unbearable, and that a man can't live inside it.

He can. That's the punchline. That's the actual, genuine punchline of the whole thing and I want it right here at the bottom of the worst chapter, because if I've done anything in this account I've been funny about it, and I'm not stopping now that it's got hard.

You'd think a hole like that in a man would kill him. It doesn't. It's just there. You get up, you have your eggs, you take your pills, you can't find the word for the flat fucking thing, you go to bed.

Guilt has a shape. Guilt you can carry, guilt has handles on it — men have carried guilt across whole continents, it's practically a piece of luggage. This has no shape at all. There's nothing to pick up.
45. The Aftermath

Nobody writes this part down. They write the fight. The fight is nine pages and this is the next two years, and I've never once read an honest account of it, so here's mine, and I've kept it in days because days is how it comes. Day 0. Somebody up top called it in from the service road, which took courage, because it ended the tunnel and everybody knew it would. Two men rode up in the cage holding me on the bar. A hundred and forty men went up that shaft six at a time in the dark before the ambulance got in past the gate and there is not one photograph of any of it and there never will be.

Bleeding on the brain. Two kinds — one fast, between the skull and the covering, which is the kind that kills you in an afternoon, and one slower underneath it. They opened my head on the left side to let the pressure off. There's a shaved patch that's never grown back right and a scar behind the ear that Colleen calls my zipper. Days 1–11. Nothing. I wasn't there. Colleen was, the whole time, from Naperville, with her husband doing the kids. She slept in a chair for eleven days. She has never once made me feel bad about it, which is the cruelest thing she could have done. Day 11. Awake. A tube in my nose, which as I've said is a design decision I'd like to raise with somebody.
I said — first words, according to Colleen, who wrote them down — "Am I in the building?"
Because I knew the ceiling. It's the building where he died. Same tiles. Day 14. The face, first look. They don't like giving you a mirror and I made them.

Both eyes shut, so Colleen held the lids. Head shaved on one side with a line of staples in it. Nose gone to the left and flat and packed. Both brows closed with something that looked like fishing line, and the right one done in two sections because there was a piece missing — missing, gone, not there, and they'd pulled the two ends together, so my right eyebrow now stops for about a centimeter in the middle. It looks like a road with a bridge out.

The left eye sitting low in the socket, and it has stayed low. The right cheek flat from May. The mouth not symmetrical anymore — the left corner doesn't come up as far as the right, so my smile now goes on at half speed on one side and I look, in photographs, permanently sarcastic. Which, in fairness.
I looked at it for a good while and I said: "Well. There goes the modeling."

Colleen laughed and then went out into the corridor for ten minutes, which is what people do around me now, and I have learned not to comment on it. Day 21. Home to Naperville, not Hegewisch, because I couldn't be alone and there was no argument about it and I didn't have one in me. Days 21–60. Here's what those weeks are, physically.
You sleep fourteen hours and wake up tired. Not sleepy. Tired, in the arms and the chest, like the tiredness after a funeral.

Light hurts. Not metaphorically. Sunlight through a window is a physical event and you go and sit in the room at the back with the blind down and everybody thinks you're depressed and you're not, you're hiding from a lamp.

Noise is worse. Two people talking at once is not two conversations, it's a substance, and it fills your head up and you have to leave the room. Colleen's kids are nine and thirteen and I love them and for two months I could not be in a kitchen with both of them.

Balance. You get up off a sofa and the room takes a second and a half to catch up, and in that second and a half you are a man on the deck of a boat, and nine times in those weeks I went down. The last one I broke a lamp and my niece cried and I said "the lamp started it," which she did not find funny and which I still maintain was good.

The headache. Behind the left eye, all day, every day, with the metal taste in it. It has never gone. It's there now. Day 40. The first real inventory of what didn't come back. Words. Nouns, mostly. Ordinary ones. I lose four or five a day and they're not hard words, they're spatula words. There's a specific horror to standing in a room holding an object and knowing you know its name and not being able to get at it, and the horror wears off. That's what nobody tells you. It wears off, and then it's just a thing you do, like limping.

Sequence. I cannot hold a sequence. Recipes are gone. Instructions are gone. A man on the phone says "go to the website, click the third tab, enter the number from the top of the letter" and by tab I have lost the website. I keep everything on paper now, in lists, in a spiral notebook, and if I lose the notebook I lose the week. Time. No sense of elapsed anything. I'll sit down and get up and it's been forty minutes or four. I set alarms to eat. Faces. Not people — faces. I know Colleen's voice instantly and I have twice failed to recognize her in a doorway. It comes back after a second. It's a second I could do without. The temper. This is the one nobody warns the family about and it's the one that costs you. It's not that I got angry. It's that the gap between the thing happening and me being enormously, violently angry about it went from about four seconds to zero. There's no runway. I went off at a supermarket cashier in March 2023 over a coupon and I heard myself from a long way away and I could not get back to the controls in time, and I went out to the parking lot and sat in the truck and cried, over a coupon, in a lot in Naperville.

I have since put a rubber band on the notebook and when I feel the zero I go outside. It works about seventy percent. Seventy percent is not a good number in the business of speaking to human beings, but it's what's on offer. What came back. Reading, mostly. Music, entirely — music is the one thing that works better than it did, which nobody has explained to me. Driving, eventually, and I take back roads. And the mouth.

That's the thing. That's the part I want to put down because it surprised me more than any of it. Every single one of the higher functions came back damaged or didn't come back — the words, the sequence, the time, the temper, the face of my own sister in a doorway — and the whole apparatus for taking the piss came through without a scratch.

I can't remember whether I've eaten. I can tell you, instantly, unerringly, at speed, that the resident who did my brows in September had a jaw like a man defusing something. I couldn't get spatula for six minutes and I got the lamp started it in under half a second with a broken head, lying on the floor of my sister's front room.

Ashkani says it's real, that it's one of the deepest things there is, that it's older and lower down than the parts that fell over. I don't know. What I know is that I lost my wife twice, and my son, and my face, and my words, and eleven minutes of the fourth of November 2017, and the last man standing in the building is the one who does the jokes.

Which is either a mercy or a joke in itself, and I've never been able to tell, and if you knew who was asking you'd know why that's funny. Day 61. Denny Fewster came to my sister's house in Naperville on the twenty-second of March, 2023, seven months to the day since he stood on my step in a windbreaker and wouldn't come past the door.
He came in. Straight past me, into the kitchen, put a bag on the counter.

He'd brought a pie. Sixty-seven years old, drove out to Naperville from South Deering with a pie. He looked at my face for a long time. "Well," he said, "you look like a thumb." "With a face drawn on it," I said. "With a face drawn on it," he said. "Yeah."

And then Denny Fewster sat down at my sister's kitchen table and put his hands flat on it and cried, which I had not seen him do at Marge's funeral and did not see him do at any point in thirty-four years, and I sat there with my head shaved on one side and my eyebrow with the bridge out and I could not do it with him.
Still can't. That's a thing I should probably tell you before we finish. I have cried three times since 2015.
A dirt floor in a barn in Will County in July, when the supply ran short. A coupon, in a parking lot in Naperville.

And once on Cicero Avenue in December of 2021, at a jingle for a mattress place, so hard I had to pull the truck over — and I have called that laughing for four years, in this account and everywhere else, and I sat down last month and worked out that I don't actually know which one it was. Not once for either of them, though. Not for her and not for him.
46. Asha
Parvaneh Ashkani sees me twice a year and has done since 2023, and she has never once said I told you, which given the circumstances is a feat of self-control I regard as roughly athletic.

The last time was in June. Parking structure out the window, same bird on the shelf, daughters a bit older in the photograph. "You've lost weight," she said. "I've lost a lot of things. The weight's the least of it." "How's the notebook?"
"The notebook's fine. The notebook is a stunning success. My problem is remembering that there's a notebook."

She wrote something down. I watched her do it and I thought: at some point somebody's going to read that file and it's going to be a hell of a read. What's left. She went through it and I'll give it to you the way she gave it to me, which is straight, because I asked her a long time ago to stop cushioning and she stopped, and it's the only relationship in my life that has actually improved.

The bleeds are done and the pressure's fine. The skull is the skull. The face is the face and there's a surgeon who could do something about the rim and the cheek and I'm not going to, because I've had enough of buildings.
The headache is permanent. The taste with it is permanent, and no, they don't know why it has a taste.
The words, the sequence, the time and the temper are not going to get much better than they got by the end of the first year, which is where they are.

And underneath all of that, running quietly, there's the other thing, the umbrella ribs coming loose and clumping and spreading, cell to cell, outward from the folds where the vessels run. Which cannot be seen in a living man. Which will be there in twenty years and will be more of it than there is now.
"So what does that look like," I said. "In ten years. Fifteen."

"I don't know," she said. "Nobody does. Anybody who tells you a timeline is selling something. What I can tell you is that in men with your exposure the things that most often go first are the temper, the judgment, the impulse control, and the mood. The parts that stop you doing things." She put the pen down. "The parts that were already, in your case, historically underfunded." "That's a joke." "It's a very small one. I've been saving it since 2022." "It was worth the wait." "It really wasn't." What's coming. Then she said the part I want on the page.
"Sean. I want to say one thing about the visits, because you're going to be an old man someday and you'll still be asking, so let's do it now while I'm here to answer.

"Do I think you saw your wife? No. I think a damaged brain produced experiences that felt more real than reality, because that's what damaged brains do, and I think the content of them was assembled out of what you needed. That's my professional opinion and I'll put it in writing.

"But I want to be honest with you about the limits of it, because you've been lied to enough, mostly by yourself. I can't test it. There's no instrument. I wasn't in there. Nobody has ever been in there but you, and the you who was in there has been altered so many times that he isn't available for questioning." She sat back. "So what I actually think is: probably a construction. And I have to live with probably, and so do you, and I've noticed over thirty years that people find probably much harder than no." "And the last one," I said. "The true one."

"That's the part I can't do anything with," she said. "Because that one's checkable, isn't it. The bags were in the car. That's on a police form. So the twelfth one lines up with the world, and the other eleven don't." She looked at me. "Which is either your brain finally coughing up the truth, or it's your brain building the version that matched the paperwork you'd read in a drawer in April." "That's the same problem again."
"It's the same problem again," she said. "It's the only problem you've got, and it doesn't have an answer, and I'd rather you heard that from me than got it off the internet at two in the morning."
The last thing.
At the end I said: "Doc. That story. The father and the son and the medicine that comes late." "Rostam and Sohrab." "I've thought about it a lot." "So has everybody for a thousand years."
"I had it wrong," I said. "In September, in the corridor. I drove home thinking it was about the king. About being late. About the medicine sitting in a room while somebody dies." "And now?"

"Now I think the boy asked him three times who he was. And every time, he could have said. And he didn't say, because he had a good reason, because he was being careful, because it was tactically sound." I had to stop and go around a word I couldn't get and come back at it from the other side, which is how I talk now, and she waited, which she always does. "He wasn't late. He had it. He had the whole thing in his hand at the start and he chose the other one, and everything after that was just the two days it took." Parvaneh Ashkani sat there for a while.
"My grandmother," she said, "would have said that's the only reading. She'd have said the medicine business is for children, so they've got something to cry about at the end." "What would you say?"
"I'd say she was a very hard woman and I miss her every day."
She stood up and shook my hand, which she does, which nobody in a hospital does. "Six months," she said. "I'll write it in the notebook." "Write it in the notebook."
47. On the Hook
I moved back to Baltimore Avenue in the spring of 2024, over Colleen's objection, which she registered in writing, which she is a lawyer's wife and does. Here's the house now.
I use six rooms. That's not nothing. Six out of eleven, up from four, which took two years and is the closest thing to progress in this entire account.

I cut the hedge. Took me nine days, at forty minutes a day, because forty minutes is what I've got before the noise of the trimmer puts me in a dark room with a blind down, and because I can't hold a sequence, so I did it in a spiral pattern with no plan and it came out looking like something an animal did. A man came past on the second day and said, "About time," and I said, "It's not finished," and he said, "It's not started," and I laughed so hard I had to go inside.

I go in the back bedroom now. There's nothing in there. That's the thing I'd been walking past for nine years — an empty room with a rocking chair in it and a shade on the window and eleven days' worth of nothing. I go in about once a month and stand there and don't feel anything at all, which is exactly what I've always been afraid of, and it turns out that once you've actually gone in and confirmed it, it costs about eight dollars a month instead of everything you own.

The tooth is in the drawer with the paperwork. So is the inventory sheet, but the inventory sheet is also on the refrigerator, unfolded, held on with a magnet from a pizza place, because I found out what my own head does to a piece of paper it doesn't like and I am not giving it the chance again. I read it every morning while the eggs go. One (1) suitcase, hardshell, blue. One (1) duffel bag, canvas, olive. One (1) box, cardboard, containing books and framed photographs.
That's my liturgy. That's what I've got instead of a prayer.

I don't know what happened to Marek Sowinski. He came to Naperville once, in April of 2023, and stood in my sister's kitchen with a broken hand still in a splint, nineteen years old, and I told him the only true thing I had, which was: You weren't in a fight. You were an instrument, and I picked you up off a sidewalk, and none of it was yours. And he said, "That's not how it works, though, is it," which is the most intelligent thing anybody has said to me in this whole business, and then he went out to his car.
I have made two attempts to find out what became of him and I stopped both times, and I'd like to tell you that was decency, and I think it was more likely the other thing.

The tunnel's shut. That specific room, anyway. Whoever it was that called it in from the service road, they came and welded the headhouse door and put a real padlock on the gate, and I have no doubt at all that within a year there was another room somewhere under this city with a bell in it, because there always is, because the demand is not for a room.

Denny comes Sundays. We watch fights on television and he tells me what's wrong with everybody and I agree with him and neither of us has ever mentioned the twenty-second of August 2022, and we've got maybe six or eight years of Sundays left between us at the current rate, and I'd trade a great deal of what I've told you in this book to keep them. Colleen calls Wednesdays. I sound flat. It's the phone.
And here's what I actually do, if you want the honest picture, rather than the tidy one.
I lie on that couch some nights and I try to make it happen.

Not the fighting. That's done — not because I found God or grew up, but because the mechanism is broken, because the room I'd need is welded shut and because I couldn't take a punch now without dying, and I want to be very clear that those are the reasons. It's not virtue. It was never going to be virtue. It ran out.

But I lie there and I try to get back into that kitchen. The night one. The real one. Eleven forty at night with the overhead on and the moths in it and the storm door shut and the pan burnt in the sink and my wife in the doorway with a bag on her shoulder saying Sean, say something.
And I go at it from every angle I've got left, and what I get is the same eleven seconds of an elastic and the word hook, and then smooth nothing where the rest of my life should be.
She doesn't come. Neither of them does. Not the accurate one and not the one in the cardigan.
That's the thing about the whole arrangement that I think I'd want somebody to know, if any of this was ever going to be any use to anybody, which it isn't.

I paid everything. Every single thing I had. Twenty-two months, fourteen fights, a face, a skull, a vocabulary, my sense of time, my sister's peace of mind, a nineteen-year-old boy's whole idea of himself, and the last copy in existence of a woman called Nuala Deane, who was funny, who was fast, who was mean as a snake and softer than anybody I ever met, who could take the roof off a room — and what I bought with it was eleven seconds of a hair elastic and the certain knowledge that I will never find out what kind of man I was in my own kitchen for eleven minutes on the fourth of November, 2017.
That's the deal. That's the whole exchange rate, finally, in writing, after two years of arithmetic. So I did the only thing left that I could do.
I took the plastic bag out of the drawer — the sealed one, with the case number on it in ballpoint — and I cut it open with scissors, and I took out her keys.
House key, car key, a key to her mother's place that hasn't fit anything since 2016, a little enamel thing off a keyring from Galway. And I put them on the hook by the back door.
They're there now. I can see them from the couch when the kitchen light's on.

I don't know why she said it. Eleven times, in eleven rooms, in eleven wrecked versions of my head, in a barn and a scrap yard and a truck bay and a room three hundred feet under this city: Sean, did you move my keys? They're not on the hook.

I built that sentence out of something. There's no random in it. Something happened in that kitchen and it went into the concrete of the thing I made, and I have no way in and no way of ever finding out and I am not going to know, and Mrs. Zabrocki heard the storm door go twice, and she's dead, and the trooper wrote one line. But they're on the hook now. Whatever it was. Whatever I did or didn't do.
They're on the hook, love. They've been on the hook the whole time.
